ideas.first_90_days: Collect findings reports for 100 past CFM56-7B visits from 2 lessors; build the forecast; back-test against actual bills of materials; sell one pilot kit with a turnaround guarantee.

ideas.title: Shop-Floor Ledger: evidence capture the MRO ERPs cannot do
ideas.one_liner: Capture shop-floor work (voice, photos, tool data) as it happens, draft the paperwork, and produce a tamper-evident evidence package lessors can rely on.
ideas.customer: Engine and component repair shops that serve lessors, then airline hangars.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The shop pays per technician per year (VP Operations / VP Quality); the pull comes from lessors and insurers who will accept the evidence package for reserve claims and release documentation.
ideas.problem: A large share of shop labor and most of a quality manager's time goes to reconciling travelers, manual revisions and release tags after the work is done (insider hypothesis, unverified). The ERP stores what was typed, not what was done, which is why records fraud is possible and why lessors re-audit shops. Oliver Wyman: 58% of MRO firms are still experimental on AI and data quality is the main barrier to scaling.
ideas.solution: Hangar-floor capture tied to the work package; draft task-card entries, findings reports and release documentation for human certifier review; tamper-evident logs. The dataset feeds Kit-First and Graded Parts. Legal premise: maintenance records need a human certifier's signature, so AI drafts are not releases; FAA AC 120-78A (electronic signatures/records) and EASA Part-145 record-keeping apply (unverified); liability and data-ownership terms must be settled.
ideas.why_now: Engines are scarce, so lessors scrutinize records and shop evidence more closely (Acumen); speech and vision models are good enough for noisy hangars; incumbents have moved only to planning (Aer Lingus signed AISmartPlan).
ideas.wedge: The findings report and release package for one engine type at shops that serve lessors. First 10 customers: five independent CFM56 shops and five component repair stations handling lessor work.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: ~800k technicians worldwide x $1,800 a year; $100M = ~55,000 seats, ~7% of technicians. Value check: documentation is ~10% of time and a technician costs $75-90k loaded, so the saving is $7-9k a year against a $1.8k price.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EmpowerMX (EMX Vision), Amygda, Soji AI, SAMIS AI, AISmartPlan, flydocs (Lufthansa Technik, lease-return records), Bluetail (business aviation records) and the ERP vendors (Trax, Ramco, AMOS and others; unverified).
ideas.why_they_lose: They sell copilots or planning to planners; none sells an evidence package a lessor accepts; ERPs sold per planner seat cannot restructure around floor capture without cannibalizing themselves.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (embedded in work packages and quality manuals) plus a data asset. Weak against ERP vendors bundling a native version.
ideas.earned_secret: The people who sign are not the people who type, and the paperwork is reconstructed after the fact, which is exactly where fraud and delay hide. A lessor-accepted evidence package creates demand pull that a generic copilot cannot (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Shadow two shops for a week and time the paperwork; build capture for one workflow (borescope findings to findings report); get a lessor to accept the output for one reserve claim.

ideas.title: Engine Lifeline: flexible-term spare-engine cover pool for institutional owners
ideas.one_liner: A neutral pool manager that serves 60-180 day cover needs from institutional owners' engines and airlines' idle spares under one standardized swap protocol.
ideas.customer: Airlines with engines in the shop and institutional owners (Bridgepoint/AIP/GFH, Sanad, credit funds) that need an operator.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Airlines pay rent (IBA: above $6,500 a day for newer engines, up from ~$5,000 in 2022-23); owners pay the manager a share of rent plus swap fees. Signer: VP Technical Operations (airline); Chief Investment Officer or asset manager (owner).
ideas.problem: Engine availability limits both deliveries and operations (Willis); shop visits take 180-300 days; airlines lease rather than overhaul $10M+ engines to preserve cash and typically sign ~3-year leases for shorter needs, then extend them (a second cost clock). Reuters: US airlines' engine spending is up ~68% from 2019 to 2025 on ~10% more flying.
ideas.solution: Aggregate 150-450 engines from several owners and airline spares into one pool with swap-ready records, standard rate cards, borescope baselines, quick-change kits, insurance, short-notice logistics and remarketing. Legal premise (unverified): Cape Town Convention registrations and title; effect of installing third-party engines on OEM warranties and LTSA coverage; customs and VAT on temporary imports; return to lease conditions.
ideas.why_now: Institutional capital just arrived: Bridgepoint/AIP/GFH launched a $1B engine platform (Oct 2026) and ordered 11 LEAP-1B spares for 2027-29 delivery; Willis reports 84% utilization and record rent; scarcity is forecast to last through 2030.
ideas.wedge: CFM56-7B and -5B first (high utilization, elevated rates), then LEAP-1A/1B. First 10 customers: four mid-tier airlines with engines in shop and three owners with idle engines.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumptions: 450-engine pool = 270 next-gen at ~$12M (~$3.2B) earning $6,500 a day at 85% utilization = $2.0M each ($545M) plus 180 legacy at ~$4M (~$0.7B) earning $45k a month = $0.46M each ($83M); total rent ~$630M. Manager fee 12% of rent = $75M plus ~1,170 swaps a year at $40k = $47M, so ~$120M. Requires ~$4B of engines under management, about four platforms the size of Bridgepoint's $1B target: heroic but plausible if institutional appetite persists.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Willis Lease (leases, 84% utilization, Q1 2026 lease rent $77M), AIP Capital (manages the Bridgepoint/GFH platform), Sanad (asset management arm, 17 engines), FTAI Aviation; unverified: AerCap/Engine Lease Finance, AerSale, GA Telesis and OEM rental pools.
ideas.why_they_lose: Principal lessors prefer long terms to protect yield and avoid swap cost; none aggregates other owners' engines or airlines' idle spares; institutional owners have no operations team and would rather outsource.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more engines, more coverage, more airlines), process power (the swap protocol) and scale economies in logistics.
ideas.earned_secret: Lessors insist on ~3-year terms because each swap costs $150-300k of records, installation and logistics work and carries return-condition risk; standardizing the swap makes 90-day cover profitable at higher day-rates and lifts utilization (insider hypothesis, unverified). Airline-owned spares sit idle ~25% of the time (unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Choose CFM56-7B; price and test a standard swap kit; sign letters with 2 owners and 3 airlines; run one live swap and measure its true cost.

ideas.title: Certifier Capacity: portable-authorization travel certifiers
ideas.one_liner: A roster of pre-vetted certifying staff with portable company authorizations, sold to hangars and line stations short of signatures.
ideas.customer: MROs, airline hangars and line stations short of certifying staff.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contract-labor and recruiting budget lines. Signer: VP Operations or Director of Maintenance.
ideas.problem: The US is short 17,800 certified mechanics in 2025, rising to 22,000 by 2027 (Oliver Wyman via McLarens); labor rates rise 5.5-6.0% a year and engine labor 6.4-8.3% by region; two-thirds of firms find hiring hard and over half expect attrition to worsen; Boeing sees 710,000 technicians needed through 2044. Every task card needs an authorized signature, so certifiers per shift cap throughput, and onboarding a contractor takes days to weeks of authorization paperwork (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.solution: Recruit and retain certifiers with retention bonds, pre-clear them against each host's quality manual, maintain a portable record of training, experience and authorization history accepted by many hosts, and add an employer-funded training pipeline. Legal premise (unverified): an A&P certificate alone does not authorize release to service in a Part 145 station; each individual must be authorized under the station's manual; FAA-EASA arrangements recognize organizations, not individual licenses; W-2 vs 1099 classification and visa limits apply.
ideas.why_now: Capacity expansions (IATA, OEM hubs) all need the same scarce people; labor is the top disruptor in Oliver Wyman's survey; employer pathways (SkyWest, Bombardier, Epic Flight Academy's $27,000 scholarship program) show employers will pay to secure supply.
ideas.wedge: US A&P with inspection authorization for engine and component shops on contract. First 10 customers: five independent engine shops and five regional hangars.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross profit, not revenue. Assumptions: bill ~$65 an hour vs pay ~$43 (Mojave posting) = $22 an hour x 1,900 hours = ~$42k per FTE, so $100M needs ~2,400 FTE and ~$300M of billings. That is ~11% of the US shortfall, ~0.3% of an estimated 800k worldwide workforce. Travel-nurse staffers (AMN, Cross Country) show the model reaches billions in revenue (unverified).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Specialist aviation staffers (for example Total Aviation Staffing); unverified: generalist staffers like Aerotek and Kelly; employer pathways (SkyWest AMT Pathway, Bombardier apprenticeship with WSU Tech, Epic Flight Academy); Part 147 schools.
ideas.why_they_lose: Staffers sell bodies, not authorization-ready certifiers; employer pipelines serve only their own demand; nobody has built a portable record that hosts accept.
ideas.moat: Weak: cornered resource in a vetted roster, switching costs from embedded authorizations and scale economies in recruiting. This is the least defensible idea and rated accordingly.
ideas.earned_secret: The binding constraint in a hangar is signatures, not hands, and onboarding delay (not scarcity of mechanics alone) keeps rosters idle; a portable competency record removes that delay. This is travel nursing for aviation (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 hangar managers on contractor onboarding time; sign 3 hosts for 20 pre-vetted certifiers; measure days saved vs a typical contract hire.

ideas.title: Last Mile: a locate-first, net-recovery operator for the default chain
ideas.one_liner: A forwarder paid on dollars recovered per defaulted dollar instead of per truck roll: it finds the car before the file is assigned, offers cooperating borrowers a scheduled hand-back, and routes each recovered unit to its best sale channel.
ideas.customer: Non-captive lenders with 8k-30k repossessions a year: independent subprime lenders, credit unions with $1B+ auto books, regional banks, private-credit-owned portfolios.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lender's SVP Collections/Recovery signs, CFO co-signs. Paid from the existing recovery line (forwarder fees, transport, storage, auction and title costs). It re-bundles spend that already exists; no new budget needed.
ideas.problem: The default chain is paid per activity, so nobody owns net proceeds. RDN data (relayed by trade press, not opened at source) show ~2.42M repossession assignments in Q2 2025 against a 29% recovery ratio (27% in 2023). That ratio includes cancellations (borrower cures), so the true skip rate is unknown (U). Lenders see only the success fee (forwarder billed $750-900, agent paid $325-375; dated), so failed attempts are invisible, and files are assigned at day 60-90, after the car has moved. Non-prime ABS recoveries averaged 38.2% in 2024 (S: KBRA, opened).
ideas.solution: (1) At day 30-45 delinquent, pre-locate the vehicle and verify lien, insurance and bankruptcy flags. (2) Offer cooperating borrowers a scheduled voluntary surrender with a defined deficiency and credit-reporting outcome. (3) Dispatch agents only to located units at a fixed price plus a first-attempt bonus. (4) Route each recovered unit by condition, mileage and title to digital wholesale, dealer direct, export or parts. (5) Decide pursue/sell/release on the deficiency by state law and borrower profile. Price: base fee below the lender's current forwarding bill plus 20-30% of net recovery above a baseline back-tested on the lender's own prior vintages.
ideas.why_now: Repossessions at multi-year highs (Cox ~1.8M expected for 2025; RDN ~2.95M annualized from 2.21M year-to-date through Q3 2025), non-prime recoveries weak, ABS investors and private credit now ask for recovery reporting, and digital remarketing channels (OPENLANE etc.) exist to plug into. Cost-pressed lenders will trade a lower fee for a recovery lift.
ideas.wedge: One lender, a 90-day randomized pilot on 1,000 defaulted accounts (treatment: pre-locate plus managed hand-back; control: current process). First ten: credit unions with $1-5B auto books (no forwarding scale, member-sensitive) and independent subprime lenders.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Lender pays ~$1,450 all-in per recovered unit today (forwarding ~$825, transport ~$250, auction/seller fees ~$300, title ~$75). We bill ~$1,000 for services we control (base $700, remarketing coordination $150, lift share $150 average), pay agents ~$350, net ~$650/unit. $100M net = ~154k units/yr ($100M gross = ~100k units): 5-9% of annual repossessions (1.8M Cox-type count to 2.95M RDN-type count), or 8-12 mid-size lenders at 12-18k repos each. Lender test: +3 points of recovery on a $17k defaulted balance = ~$510/unit; our lift share is under a third of it. Share is high but under 20%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Primeritus (forwarding, skip tracing, remarketing; formed 2012 by Kinderhook; sold its direct recovery arm to Connect 1 Recovery; 2026 status unverified), the RDN assignment network, MBSi (remarketing and VINchex lien checks), OPENLANE and Manheim digital repo programs, Servicing Solutions, regional forwarders, in-house recovery at the largest lenders. Motorola's DRN plate-read data is the likely locate source (U).
ideas.why_they_lose: Forwarders earn per assignment and per success, so they gain from volume and cannot underwrite outcomes; the RDN network is a pipe, not an operator; auctions earn on lane sales and fees, not net proceeds; inside a lender, collections, recovery, remarketing and legal are separate cost centers with separate vendors, so no one is paid on the net number.
ideas.moat: Process power (per-unit outcome data becomes a recovery-pricing engine nobody else has), counter-positioning against activity-priced forwarders, scale economies in dispatch density.
ideas.earned_secret: Insider = 20-year repo forwarder/remarketing manager. Repossession is a timing and information business, not a muscle business. Most assignments never end in a car on a truck, but the lender never sees that because it pays only on success and the forwarder bakes failure into the success fee. Every link is paid per activity (forwarder per recovery, agent per grab, yard per day, auction per sale, agency per deficiency dollar); no one is paid on net proceeds per defaulted dollar. A cooperating borrower who hands the car back on a scheduled day costs a fraction of a field repo and the car arrives cleaner (A).
ideas.first_90_days: Pull the public RDN/Cox series; hire a former forwarder ops head; contract ~50 agencies under a standard compliance pack; sign one mid-size lender for the 1,000-account randomized pilot; measure recovery ratio, days to sale and net proceeds vs control. Legal checks: state repossession-agency licensing, UCC 9-609 breach of peace, FDCPA 1692f(6), DPPA permissible use for plate data (U), voluntary surrender must be genuinely voluntary.

ideas.title: Downshift: a lender-approved short-payoff and trade-down exchange
ideas.one_liner: Before the repossession, a delinquent borrower is matched with a dealer that buys the car near retail value and puts them in a cheaper one, with the lender pre-approving the short payoff: the auto version of a mortgage short sale.
ideas.customer: Lenders' loss-mitigation teams (subprime, credit unions, captives' used books) and independent/BHPH dealers who want inventory and customers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lender SVP Collections/Loss Mitigation pays a per-completed-case fee from recovery and charge-off budgets; the dealer pays a car-acquisition fee. Lender's CRO or Head of Servicing signs the short-payoff policy.
ideas.problem: A repossession destroys value: non-prime recovery averages 38.2% (S), the borrower loses transport and income stability, and the lender books a deficiency it rarely collects. About 31% of new-car trade-ins are underwater (Edmunds via a vendor; pool file) and 35.55% of new loans run longer than six years, so the number of upside-down borrowers is large. No lender-integrated mechanism accepts a short payoff; auto 'short sale' exists only as an informal, discretionary request (search found no lender policy documents).
ideas.solution: A standard short-payoff product. The lender pre-authorizes a window (accept up to X% of appraised value as payoff in full or partial, residual released or sold as an unsecured balance). The platform matches the borrower to a partner dealer that appraises, buys the car, pays off the lien and sells a lower-payment vehicle financed by the dealer's own lender. The platform handles lien payoff, paperwork, credit-reporting codes, Form 1099-C where debt is forgiven (U) and a compliance audit trail.
ideas.why_now: Record serious delinquency, record negative equity, long terms (pool file), a used market firm enough that cars hold value, and private-credit owners of loans who want fewer deficiencies. BHPH loans are in active repossession at 16.63 times the rate of traditional lenders (S: Fed FEDS note, opened), showing how much BHPH dealers already repossess and resell.
ideas.wedge: Two lenders with in-house repo programs plus five BHPH/independent dealers in one metro; run 200 swaps against matched repossession cohorts. First ten: credit unions and independent subprime lenders that already run voluntary-surrender programs.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Balance $18k; repossession at the 38.2% recovery rate returns $6.9k, less ~$1.45k of costs = ~$5.4k net. Short payoff: dealer pays ~$8.0k (it can retail the car), lender pays a $700 fee = ~$7.3k net, a gain of ~$1.9k per case. Platform revenue per case = $700 lender + $300 dealer = $1,000. $100M = 100k completed cases a year = 3.4-5.6% of annual repossessions (1.8M-2.95M), or ~11% of the ~0.9M loans 60+ days delinquent (6.9% x 13M). Under 20% share, but sourcing the volume is the hard part.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Informal BHPH dealers; 'we buy any car' retailers (Carvana, CarMax) that pay off liens but make the borrower cover negative equity; lender hardship teams (extensions, deferrals, modifications). No packaged marketplace found. I did not search lender policy documents, so this is 'not found', not 'does not exist'.
ideas.why_they_lose: Lender loss-mitigation systems are built for modifications and extensions, not asset sales; big used-car buyers have no reason to absorb a lender's loss; ABS servicing agreements limit modifications and a short payoff may need servicer or trustee consent (U), which is exactly the standardization a platform sells.
ideas.moat: Network economies (lender pre-authorizations on one side, dealer inventory and appetite on the other), then switching costs once the lender's policy engine integrates.
ideas.earned_secret: Insider = BHPH dealer principal, 20 years. 'The best loss mitigation is selling the customer a cheaper car, not taking back the one they cannot afford. I buy their car, put them in a $9k car at $60 a week and keep them current. A bank can't: the loan is upside down, it has no way to accept a short payoff, no replacement inventory and no retail channel.' Rolling negative equity into a new loan is reported to more than double repossession odds (secondary report of a CFPB finding; U).
ideas.first_90_days: Get one lender's actual repossession-vs-swap economics from its own data; line up five dealers; draft the short-payoff policy with the lender's counsel (check ABS consent, 1099-C, state deficiency and notice law, UDAAP and fair-lending risk on the replacement loan, dealer adverse selection); run the 200-case pilot.

ideas.title: Policy Escrow: the car's insurance inside the car payment
ideas.one_liner: Mortgage lenders solved uninsured collateral with escrow; auto lenders never did. A licensed, carrier-neutral agency collects the premium with the loan payment, keeps coverage continuous, and feeds policy status to the lender.
ideas.customer: Non-prime auto lenders, credit unions and BHPH dealers, plus non-standard carriers that want low-lapse distribution.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Carriers pay commission (10-15%; U). The lender pays nothing and gets lower collateral risk, a policy-status data feed and a replacement for clunky tracking/force-placement. Lender's Head of Collateral or CRO signs the integration.
ideas.problem: The two biggest bills of a subprime borrower, the car payment and the premium, compete, and the one that breaks first takes the other with it. Subprime portfolios run 35-40% uninsured vs 10-15% for prime (S, dated vendor data). Lender-placed coverage is expensive and narrow, and the vendors that sell it earn more when borrowers lapse.
ideas.solution: Optional, multi-carrier policy escrow: at origination or at the first 30-day miss, the borrower can fold a quoted non-standard policy into one monthly draft. The agency pays the carrier, bridges a late premium out of the next payment, and gives the lender real-time coverage status. Premium financing and the payment draft run on state-compliant rails.
ideas.why_now: Insurance costs are surging, subprime delinquency is at a record, and embedded insurance is moving: Deloitte forecasts up to a fifth of personal auto insurance embedded in vehicle sales by 2030, with Root-Carvana cited as an example (S). The one direct competitor found (Gaya) shows $50K raised.
ideas.wedge: One credit union or BHPH group with its own force-placement data; start with 30-day-delinquent 'insurance-first' outreach, then move to origination. First ten: credit unions and BHPH groups with 20k+ loans.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A/U) ~13M non-prime loans x ~$3,000 premium (U) = ~$39B of premiums; at 12% commission (U) the pool is ~$4.7B. $100M of commission = ~$830M of premium = ~277k policies = ~2% of non-prime loans. Three to five lenders with 100k+ loans each, or a few hundred BHPH/credit-union partners. Share needed is small; the constraints are integration speed and licensing.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Gaya (tiny: $50K raised per CB Insights; sells through insurance agents), Root-Carvana embedded, Ford Credit's commercial program, lender-placed insurers (Assurant; Allstate's National General Lender Services; U), insurance-tracking vendors (Verifacto and others), and non-standard carriers selling via agents or direct.
ideas.why_they_lose: Carriers cannot sell into the lender channel without a fight with their own agents; force-placement vendors profit from lapses; lenders cannot sell insurance, cannot require a particular insurer, and have no licensed agency.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (the premium lives in the payment stream), counter-positioning against agent-channel carriers and lapse-profiting CPI vendors, and a cornered resource in lender integrations plus the policy data feed.
ideas.earned_secret: Pattern = 'control the repayment channel' (lender owns the one recurring payment the borrower protects; mortgage escrow is the proven analogue). Told from a subprime collections manager's seat (causal claim is mine to test, U): the insurance cancels first, then the payment bounces, and the lender learns the car was totalled and uninsured only when the borrower calls. Why it has not happened: lenders cannot hold an insurance license and carriers do not sell through lenders.
ideas.first_90_days: Get anonymized force-placement and lapse-to-delinquency timing from one lender and test the 'insurance lapses before the payment' claim; partner with an existing agency/MGA rather than licensing; pilot with 5,000 borrowers. Legal checks: agency licensing in every state, premium-finance and tying rules, premium trust accounting, Reg Z finance-charge treatment of a combined draft (U); keep it optional and multi-carrier.

ideas.title: Driveway in a Box: a captive finance arm for mid-size dealer groups
ideas.one_liner: Lithia and AutoNation proved a dealer group can capture the finance spread it gives away to banks; build the rest of the top ~150 groups their own captive (licensing, underwriting, servicing, funding) as a service.
ideas.customer: Dealer groups with 10k-60k retail units a year.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Group CFO/president signs; paid from the group's finance profit pool (reserve and F&I it already earns plus spread it newly keeps).
ideas.problem: A group sends each financed customer to a bank for a reserve of roughly 1-2 rate points (U) and loses the interest margin. Lithia's Driveway Finance earned a total interest margin of $58.9M in Q1 2026 on $5.0B of average managed receivables, ~4.7% annualized (S, Lithia release opened, plus my arithmetic).
ideas.solution: Multi-tenant captive stack: sales-finance licensing, decisioning, funding (pooled warehouse and ABS shelf plus forward-flow from private credit), servicing (via idea 6), collections and compliance. The dealer group keeps 60-70% of the spread and a first-loss slice for alignment; the platform charges a servicing/platform fee plus a share of finance operations income.
ideas.why_now: Proof from two public groups: DFC originated $840M at 18.0% penetration (average FICO 750) with finance operations income up 70.4% to $21.3M in Q1 2026 (S, primary); AutoNation Finance penetration rose to 11.1% from 10.0% (S, 10-Q) with a portfolio reported at $2.67B, +52% (U). Private-credit capital is abundant (TPG-OneMain $2.4B forward flow) and banks are tightening credit boxes.
ideas.wedge: Three to five 20-60 store groups; model their actual funded deals from the DMS for the last 12 months to show spread capture. First ten: groups with 20k-60k units a year and a finance-literate CFO.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) DFC's finance operations income is ~$85M a year (1.7% of $5.0B). Platform take: 0.70% of managed receivables plus 20% of finance operations income (0.34%) = ~1.0%. $100M needs ~$10B of managed receivables, about two DFCs. A 25k-unit group at 15% penetration and $30k average originates ~$112M a year and carries ~$280M at a 2.5-year life, so ~35 such groups. Against a universe I could not source (U; ~150 groups with 10k+ units), that is ~20-25%: heroic and the weakest part of the idea. It works if the first customers are larger groups.
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house captives (Lithia DFC, AutoNation Finance, CarMax Auto Finance, Carvana, DriveTime/Bridgecrest); origination/DMS vendors that route to lenders (Dealertrack, RouteOne, CDK, Reynolds); servicing software (Fiserv, Dealertrack Servicing; U).
ideas.why_they_lose: RouteOne (captive-owned; U) and Dealertrack (Cox) earn when dealers send deals to lenders and cannot help dealers disintermediate their own customers; banks pay reserve to keep dealers in the agency role; DMS vendors avoid credit and licensing.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in pooled funding and servicing, switching costs (licenses, systems, seasoned portfolios), counter-positioning against lender-routing networks.
ideas.earned_secret: Pattern = concentrated-operator vertical platform. A captive is not a credit-skill business; it is a cost-of-capital, customer-data and servicing business, and all three can be rented. Dealers already run producer-owned reinsurance on F&I insurance (U), so the structure is familiar, and the group keeps the customer and the repossessed car for resale (a BHPH-style loss recovery a distant lender loses). Why not yet: licensing, funding and servicing were each too heavy for a mid-size group alone.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick three groups; run the spread-capture model on their funded deals; get a forward-flow term sheet from a private-credit manager; hire ex-DFC/ANF/CarMax leaders; map state sales-finance licensing. Legal checks: ECOA/FCRA adverse action, reserve disclosure, ABS risk retention, funding covenants.

ideas.title: Payday Rail: lender-paid, payday-aligned payments with portable mandates
ideas.one_liner: A payment layer that asks for the car payment the day the paycheck lands (request-for-payment or pay-by-bank), retries around payday, carries no borrower fee, and keeps the payment mandate portable if the servicer changes.
ideas.customer: Non-prime lenders, credit unions and captives.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Lender's Head of Payments/Servicing Operations pays a fee per payment plus a share of failed-payment recovery; General Counsel is the champion because of pay-to-pay litigation.
ideas.problem: Bounced debits and pay-to-pay fees hurt both sides. Bridgecrest's own ABS prospectus says delinquencies vary by day of week because many borrowers pay bi-weekly (S, SEC 424B5 via search). Nacha allows at most two re-presentments of an insufficient-funds debit in 180 days (2018 Q&A; U). Pay-to-pay fees are in court: the Eleventh Circuit affirmed FDCPA liability against Ocwen over Speedpay fees (Feb 2025), courts are split, the CFPB withdrew its position in May 2025, and NACA sued GM Financial on 5/19/2026 in D.C. Superior Court, No. 2026-CAB-003388 (S, NACA page opened).
ideas.solution: Pay-by-bank/RTP/FedNow request-for-payment to the borrower on or just after a payroll-derived payday, with smart retry, account validation, card account-updater, a fee-free default path and a hardship hook. Mandates sit in a neutral layer so a servicer switch does not stop autopay. Revenue: a lender-paid fee per payment, a percentage of recovered failed payments, and float on funds in transit.
ideas.why_now: Request-for-payment is live on FedNow and RTP (S, secondary article; participation counts unverified), pay-by-bank is growing, pay-to-pay litigation is moving to state consumer-protection law now that the CFPB stepped back, and Tricolor showed what a payment-collection failure looks like.
ideas.wedge: One mid-size lender; shadow-test payday-aligned presentment for 10,000 borrowers using payroll connections (Pinwheel/Plaid-type). First ten: credit unions and subprime lenders with bi-weekly-heavy books.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) ~1.0B scheduled payments a year (85M loans x 12) plus more for weekly/bi-weekly borrowers. At $0.65 lender-paid per payment, $100M needs ~154M payments, ~15% of all scheduled payments. Add recovery fees: 60M non-prime payments with 12% failing x $550 = ~$4B failed; improving 7-day cure by 20 points pulls ~$0.8B forward; a 3% fee is ~$24M. Roughly 9-15% of payment volume. Main risk: fee compression, since lenders pay ~$0.20-0.30 per ACH today (U).
ideas.who_does_it_today: ACI Speedpay, Paymentus (markets an auto-finance product), PayNearMe, Fiserv, Jack Henry, servicers' own portals, and pay-by-bank providers such as Trustly and Plaid (U).
ideas.why_they_lose: Speedpay-style economics rest on fees borrowers pay and that lenders often share (U); removing them removes revenue, and the litigation exposure sits with the lender, not the processor. Legacy servicing platforms fix due dates and retries by schedule, not by payday.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (mandates and servicing-platform integrations), data (a payday-cadence model per borrower), counter-positioning against fee-funded processors.
ideas.earned_secret: From a subprime collections manager: delinquency is partly a calendar problem. Lenders fix the due date and retry on a schedule that ignores payday, each bounce triggers a call, a fee and a worse next month, and the day since payday predicts a bounce better than a credit score does. The tell is a mid-week spike in delinquency tapes (Bridgecrest).
ideas.first_90_days: Run the shadow test; sign a credit union and one subprime lender to a pay-by-bank pilot; get counsel's opinion on pay-to-pay exposure to use as the sales hook. Legal checks: Nacha and Reg E authorization for recurring and RfP debits, TCPA for payday prompts, state payment-fee laws, UDAAP if debits are timed to cause overdraft (RfP requires borrower approval).

ideas.title: Independent Servicer of Record ('Cenlar for auto')
ideas.one_liner: A bank-grade, multi-tenant subservicer for non-bank originators, dealer-group captives and private-credit-owned loans, so the backup servicer is already the servicer when an originator fails.
ideas.customer: Dealer-group captives (idea 4), fintech originators, private-credit funds and forward-flow buyers, small lenders that want to stop running servicing.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The originator's COO/CFO or the fund's Head of Asset Finance, from the servicing and operations budget; investors and warehouse banks increasingly require it as a covenant.
ideas.problem: Originator-servicers cannot be independent of themselves: servicing fees (several percent of balance in non-prime ABS; U) are the originator's profit and its control over collections. Backups are names on a page: Vervent, the designated backup servicer, needed 8 business days to operate inside Tricolor's legacy system and 14 to board ~100k loans (S, vendor claims), and a backup does nothing about falsified data.
ideas.solution: A multi-tenant servicing platform and licensed operations: payments, collections, hardship, title, compliance and investor reporting, with each portfolio mirrored daily. Per-loan monthly fee, lower for hot-standby-only. The successor event becomes a feature: a failed originator's portfolio moves with no migration.
ideas.why_now: Dealer-group captives (DFC, AutoNation Finance), fintech originators and forward-flow buyers are all new buyers of servicing, and Tricolor made independence a requirement. The ABA article recommends triparty servicing with cash sweeps, a verification agent and a hot backup servicer (S).
ideas.wedge: Two or three fintech/dealer-group portfolios of ~20k loans; a hot-standby contract on one warehouse facility. First ten: newer originators with no servicing DNA.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Blended fee of $7 per loan per month (not sourced; test in RFPs) = $84 a year. $100M = ~1.2M loans, ~1.4% of 85M open loans. Pipeline: DFC ~200k loans ($5.0B at $25k), AutoNation Finance ~105k, a Tricolor-sized event ~100k, plus fintech and private-credit portfolios: about 12 portfolios of 100k. Margins thin (10-15% EBITDA, A) and sales cycles long.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Vervent (backup-first, capital-markets services), Loan Portfolio Servicing (tiny, 2012-era), Bridgecrest (DriveTime's captive servicer; not pursuing outside clients at the time of the article), Westlake (U), software vendors (Fiserv, Dealertrack Servicing), BPOs, Salient (AI loan servicing, $60M Series A, July 2025; paywalled, U).
ideas.why_they_lose: Originators cannot outsource their own borrowers; software vendors will not take regulatory servicing liability; BPOs lack lender-grade licensing and compliance; Vervent's brand is a backup-servicer brand, and the one case study is a failure event.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in cost per loan, switching costs (servicing transfers are painful), process power (compliance across 50 states).
ideas.earned_secret: Told from an ABS investor's chair: after Tricolor, deals ask for a 'hot' backup servicer, but what works is a servicer that already holds a daily mirror of the data and the borrower relationship. In mortgages, subservicers (Cenlar-type, U) took servicing out of originators' hands; auto has no equivalent at scale because originators treated servicing as profit and control. New entrants (dealer captives, fintechs, funds) have no such attachment.
ideas.first_90_days: List the 30 largest new auto originators that do not own servicing; price a 20k-loan pilot; secure state servicing and collection licenses; check ABS servicing-agreement consents and FDCPA/Reg F status. The most conventional idea here, included because it is the most reachable $100M.

ideas.title: Pledge Registry: a neutral cross-lender collateral ledger with an insured certificate
ideas.one_liner: After Tricolor, a neutral registry where warehouse lenders, ABS trustees and forward-flow buyers register hashed VINs and e-chattel-paper control so a double pledge is caught before it is funded, plus an insurer-backed certificate for registered paper.
ideas.customer: Warehouse banks, private-credit funds, ABS trustees and auto originators.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Originators pay (the way a buyer pays mortgage title insurance) to win a higher advance rate; banks and funds make registration a covenant. Signers: Head of Asset-Based Finance/CRO at the lender, Treasurer/CFO at the originator.
ideas.problem: Tricolor allegedly pledged ~$2.2B of purported assets against ~$1.4B of real collateral (~$800M bogus), with ~$923M owed to lenders at bankruptcy; founder indicted (S, allegations as described in a law-firm article, opened). The controls proposed afterward (lien searches, custodians, cash sweeps, verification agents) are each lender-specific, and none sees across facilities. The ABA article itself notes lien searches miss possession or control perfection.
ideas.solution: (1) Hashed-VIN registry using private set intersection so lenders share only duplicates; (2) continuous matching of the named lienholder against state ELT records through the ELT providers; (3) registration of 'control' for e-chattel paper across vendors' vaults (eOriginal, Dealertrack, SecureClose), like the MERS eRegistry for mortgage eNotes (U); (4) monitoring of lien releases, title-absent status and bank-statement vs servicer-remittance reconciliation; (5) an insurer-backed Collateral Integrity Certificate priced like title insurance.
ideas.why_now: Tricolor and First Brands (Sept 2025), a live indictment, Wolters Kluwer and Rithm Capital arguing for continuous asset-level verification and shared registries, and a new collateral-monitoring seed round (CORA, Sept 2026) show the budget exists.
ideas.wedge: A one-time hashed-VIN overlap test run by three warehouse banks and two originators; the overlap count is the sales headline. First ten: warehouse desks at banks and ABF funds that lent to Tricolor-type borrowers.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) ~$250B auto ABS outstanding (2-year life on $127B/yr issuance, S: S&P) plus ~$150B of warehouse, forward-flow and bank-pledged paper = ~$400B, ~20M loans at ~$20k. Registry fee $3.50/loan/yr = $70M. Certificate: 0.30% premium (no market price exists, A) on 40% of ~$150B newly pledged non-bank balances = ~$180M premium; our 20% share = ~$36M. Total ~$106M needs more than half of pledged loans on the registry and 40% certificate uptake: heroic, plausible only if a bank-led covenant sets a market standard. Adding other serial-numbered collateral (RVs, boats, equipment) makes it realistic but is outside this pool. Verdict: borderline.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Custodians and e-vaults (Wolters Kluwer's eOriginal, Dealertrack's vault, SecureClose), ELT providers (Dealertrack in 37 states, VINtek, DDI, PDP, Secure Title Administration), MBSi/VINchex (lien checks for repossession, Feb 2026), Black Book vehicle verification, CORA (monitoring), field-exam and accounting firms. I found no cross-lender registry and no insurer product for double-pledged collateral.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each sees only its own customers and slice; vault vendors are competitors and cannot register each other's control; rating agencies and trustees are issuer-paid; bureaus see people, not collateral. Cross-lender sharing needs a neutral party trusted by lenders who will not hand each other their VIN lists.
ideas.moat: Network economies (each added lender raises the chance of catching a duplicate and a late entrant cannot copy the coverage) plus a cornered resource in neutrality and data. The MERS eRegistry is the precedent.
ideas.earned_secret: From an ABS analyst's seat: trustees, raters and custodians each check their own slice and rely on servicer reports. For motor vehicles the lien is perfected by title notation, not a UCC filing, so there is no central place to look. The only way to catch a duplicate is a neutral party that sees all lenders at once, and nobody was paid to be that party.
ideas.first_90_days: Run the overlap test; sign letters of intent with two vault vendors; get a Lloyd's/MGA view on certificate pricing; get a legal opinion on registering control. Legal checks: UCC 9-105 control and 9-311 title-notation perfection mean a registry detects but does not perfect; antitrust and confidentiality (hashed, aggregate-only); insurability of a certificate (U).

ideas.title: Seasoned-Paper Exchange: sell the loans that survived a year
ideas.one_liner: BHPH dealers and small lenders originate at 20%+ APR, season each loan for 12 months, and sell the performing ones, verified and registered, to credit unions, banks and private credit, recycling the dealer's capital.
ideas.customer: Sellers: BHPH dealers and independent non-bank lenders. Buyers: credit unions (refinance the borrower at a lower rate), banks, private-credit funds.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The buyer's Head of Indirect/Consumer Lending or ABF desk pays ~1% of balance; the dealer or lender CFO pays ~0.5% and gets liquidity, a bounty and the customer relationship.
ideas.problem: Banks and funds will not underwrite a single BHPH dealer; dealers cannot raise cheap capital; borrowers who have proven themselves stay at 24-29% APR. BHPH balances tripled to ~$32B between 2018 Q1 and 2025 Q3, and BHPH loans default at ~1.9 times and enter active repossession at 16.6 times the rate of traditional lenders (S: Fed FEDS note, opened). Non-prime auto ABS issuance fell 27.8% early in 2026 (S, JPMorgan data via trade press).
ideas.solution: Verification and registration (idea 7), standardized servicing data (idea 6), dealer-level seasoning scorecards, and two exits: assignment to private credit at a premium, or refinance into a credit-union loan with a dealer bounty.
ideas.why_now: The funding squeeze above, forward-flow deals proving private credit wants non-prime auto (TPG-OneMain $2.4B), and ad-hoc trades such as Westlake's ~$100M sale to HFC Acceptance (Jan 2026).
ideas.wedge: Ten BHPH dealers with 1,000+ active accounts and two credit unions; collect 12 months of payment history and build the scorecard. First ten: dealers who need capital to grow inventory.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) BHPH originations ~$18-22B a year (assuming a ~1.5-year balance life on $32B); loans current at month 12 are ~40% of originations at ~70% of balance = $5-6B. Add ~$90B of other independent non-bank balances (A) for ~$15B of graduates. Flow ~$20B/yr. Take 1.5% (1.0% buyer, 0.5% seller) = $300M at 100%; $100M needs ~$6.7B sold, about a third of the flow. Heroic. Improves if fintech originators' seasoned paper is included.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Pagaya (AI network and forward flow; buys fresh volume from partners), forward-flow programs (TPG-OneMain), ad-hoc whole-loan sales (Westlake-HFC), everchain exchange (deficiency paper), BHPH dealers' own bank lines.
ideas.why_they_lose: Forward-flow buyers want fresh volume from scaled originators; banks cannot diligence BHPH dealers; credit unions cannot reach them. No one sells a standardized, verified, seasoned product.
ideas.moat: Network economies (dealer supply and buyer demand) and a cornered resource in dealer-level seasoning data.
ideas.earned_secret: From a BHPH principal's cash-flow seat: the first year decides the loan. A loan that has made 12 payments is far safer than one that has made two, but the dealer's capital is tied up at 12-15% (U) and cannot recycle into the next sale. Cumulative-loss curves in non-prime pools are front-loaded (U), so buying at month 12 removes most of the risk while the yield stays high.
ideas.first_90_days: Collect 12 months of payment history from five dealers; build the seasoning scorecard; get an indicative bid from one credit union and one private-credit buyer. Legal checks: lender or broker licensing, Reg Z assignment and refinance disclosures, FCRA, UDAP around captive BHPH customers; dealers may resist losing customers.

ideas.title: Approved-Claim Notes
ideas.one_liner: Advance 80-90% of a contractor's invoice within 48 hours of the carrier approving it, underwritten on the carrier's obligation and repaid into a controlled account, not on the contractor's credit.
ideas.customer: Insurance-driven roofing and restoration contractors ($1-20M revenue; about 15-25k firms, my assumption) plus the PE platforms and franchise systems that roll them up.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The contractor pays 2.5-3.5% per advance (about 13-18% APR at 70 days) from its financing/working-capital expense line; signer is the owner or controller/CFO. Capital comes from warehouse lines, later forward-flow credit funds.
ideas.problem: Carrier and TPA payment now takes 60-90 days (Cotality 2026); only about 4% of contractors see insurance money in 1-2 weeks (C&R survey). Checks are held by homeowners and mortgagees, and general factors will not buy the paper because they cannot tell approved from pending or whether the check will be intercepted.
ideas.solution: Underwrite the carrier's obligation: ingest the approved estimate and carrier/TPA status, signed direction-to-pay, mortgagee status and license/permit match; advance within 48 hours of approval; route repayment to a controlled account (ties to the escrow idea); price by cross-carrier pay-speed data.
ideas.why_now: Claim volume fell about 20% in 2025 and carrier scrutiny and delay rose; digital endorsement rails (Checkbook/sureti, iink) now exist; credit funds want short-duration carrier-credit paper. Roof ACV schedules (60% of top-10 carrier policies) make depreciation non-recoverable, so the early-money product must key off approval and completion, not recoverable depreciation.
ideas.wedge: Storm-heavy roofers (TX, CO, MN) and TPA-dependent water-mitigation shops. First product only on carrier-approved invoices with a signed direction-to-pay; first 10 customers are contractors billing $300k+/month to carriers whose pay behavior we can model.
ideas.path_to_100m: At about 3% per advance, $100M needs about $3.3B of annual advances, roughly 6% of ~$57B contractor-bound claim dollars (70% of $82B, my assumption), about $630M outstanding at a 70-day turn. That is about 3-5k active contractors at $0.7-1M advanced a year, 15-25% of insurance-heavy firms. Honest caveat: this is a lender; after ~7.5% cost of funds and 0.5-1% losses, $100M of revenue is roughly $20-35M pre-tax. The durable asset is the pay-speed dataset.
ideas.who_does_it_today: National Claims Funding, ClaimPay, iink's contractor advance program, sureti (Checkbook, $3.25M raised), general factors (Triumph, Bluevine, Fundbox, Riviera), distributor trade credit (Beacon, SRS, ABC Supply), contractors' own cash.
ideas.why_they_lose: They sit outside the carrier and servicer payment flow, cannot control where the money lands, and have no cross-carrier pay-speed or dispute data; the funded ones are tiny (sureti $3.25M raised in total).
ideas.moat: Scale economies (cost of capital falls with volume, warehouse to ABS) plus cornered resource (cross-carrier pay-speed and dispute dataset).
ideas.earned_secret: What predicts payment is not the contractor's credit but four documents: a carrier-acknowledged approved estimate, a signed direction-to-pay, a mortgagee path, and a license/permit match. Contractors will pay 2-3% for two-day cash because the alternative is merchant-cash-advance pricing.
ideas.first_90_days: Weeks 1-3: get 24 months of invoice and payment history from 10 contractors (free AR dashboard) to model days-to-pay by carrier/TPA. Weeks 4-8: line up a $5M warehouse and fund $1-2M against approved estimates with direction-to-pay, one carrier family at a time. Weeks 9-13: add controlled-account repayment. Target 25 contractors, $10M advanced, losses under 1%.

ideas.title: Restoration RCM
ideas.one_liner: R1 for roofers and restorers: take over estimates, supplements, TPA invoice submission and collections, paid a percentage of what is actually collected.
ideas.customer: Insurance-heavy roofing and restoration firms, franchise groups and PE-backed platforms with $3-300M of carrier-paid billings.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contractor pays 3-5% of collected carrier/TPA dollars out of office staff, offshore estimating desks and collections cost; signer is the owner/GM, or the CFO or operating partner of a PE platform.
ideas.problem: Getting paid has overtaken labor as restoration's top concern (Cotality 2026). Each TPA has its own pricing program, documentation rules and portal; 64% of restoration firms depend on TPAs and 61% would not recommend them; carriers are buying AI to cut invoices (NovaData's carrier-side invoice review). Money leaks through short-pays and supplements nobody follows up (insider hypothesis).
ideas.solution: Managed service plus software: build estimates and supplements to each carrier/TPA's rules, submit, chase, dispute and book the collected outcome. Zero base fee; paid a share of collections; every short-pay reason is logged to a shared dataset.
ideas.why_now: Carrier-side AI desk review makes defense necessary, claim volume down 20% in 2025 pushed carriers to scrutinize every line, and LLMs cut the labor cost enough to price on outcomes.
ideas.wedge: PE-backed and franchise groups with 5-30 locations in TX, FL and CO; start on TPA-program water jobs. First 10 customers are five design-partner platforms plus five franchise groups.
ideas.path_to_100m: At 3.5-4% of collections, $100M needs about $2.5-2.9B collected, about 5% of ~$57B contractor-bound claim dollars (my assumption). That is about 12 PE platforms at $100-250M each plus roughly 700 independents at $2-3M. Low share needed, but services margins at first.
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house office staff and estimators, offshore estimate/supplement desks, Rebuild ($13M Series A, Sept 2026), Xcelerate, Cotality DASH/Symbility, JobNimbus/AccuLynx, Albiware. Healthcare RCM firms (R1, Ensemble) have not entered restoration (none found).
ideas.why_they_lose: Software vendors sell seats and leave the labor and follow-up with the contractor; offshore desks bill hours and see only one contractor's files; Rebuild focuses on generating estimates. Nobody owns the collected-dollar outcome across carriers.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (cross-carrier short-pay and denial dataset) plus process power; scale later.
ideas.earned_secret: The money is not in winning the job but in the invoice that survives desk review. Roughly 15-25% of a restoration firm's AR sits in 'pending supplement' purgatory because nobody owns the follow-up, and the shortfall is booked as 'concessions' (unverified insider hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign five design partners with $10-50M of carrier billings, including one PE platform and one franchise group. Take supplements, invoicing and AR follow-up at 4% of collected, log every short-pay reason, and by day 90 show a collected-rate lift of 5-8 points and 15 fewer days of DSO on matched jobs.

ideas.title: Storm Pro Co-op
ideas.one_liner: A free scope-and-supplement engine for insurance roofers and restorers, funded by the manufacturers and distributors who want complete systems specified, with a buying group on the same members.
ideas.customer: About 25-40k insurance-driven roofing and restoration contractors (my assumption), starting with PE-backed regional platforms.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Manufacturers (VP Residential Roofing / contractor marketing) and distributors (SVP Pro sales) pay sponsorship plus 1.5-2% admin fees on member purchases; budget lines are loyalty rebates, co-op marketing and technical services.
ideas.problem: Insurer scopes omit code-required and warranty-required components; contractors lack time and citations; manufacturers lose system sales; the three largest roofers hold under 5% of the market, so no contractor has buying power. Rebuild claims +12% reimbursement from better estimates (company claim, unverified).
ideas.solution: A free estimate and supplement engine citing code, manufacturer installation requirements and carrier guidelines, exporting to Xactimate. Sponsor items are flagged and included only where code or warranty requires them. A buying group routes member volume to chosen distributors.
ideas.why_now: Claims down 20% and roof ACV schedules (about -30% severity per Aon) shrink insured volume, so suppliers fight for attach rates; QXO bought Beacon and Home Depot bought SRS, so national programs now have central buyers; AI makes the engine cheap enough to give away.
ideas.wedge: One founding manufacturer sponsor, one product family (shingle systems), one region; 300 contractors recruited through three PE-backed platforms as the first customers.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $5B of member purchases at 1.7% is $85M, plus $15-20M of sponsorship. $5B is about 25% of the roughly $20B of insured-job materials (my estimate from roof claims of ~$31B and Beacon's $35B roofing distribution market); heroic, though buying co-ops of that size exist in hardware.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Rebuild, Xcelerate, JobNimbus/AccuLynx, EagleView/Hover measurements, GAF Rewards and Owens Corning contractor programs, distributor portals (SRS One, Beacon Pro+), regional buying groups.
ideas.why_they_lose: Software vendors charge the contractor, which caps adoption; manufacturer loyalty programs reward volume, not claim-readiness; distributors cannot be neutral between brands; none spans all brands and all carriers.
ideas.moat: Network economies (member volume buys better terms, which attracts members) plus scale economies.
ideas.earned_secret: System warranties require matching components, so a sponsor is not buying bias; it is paying to make code and warranty citations complete, which adjusters pay when asked. Roughly 25-40% of supplement dollars are standard omitted items (unverified insider hypothesis).
ideas.first_90_days: Build the code-and-manufacturer-requirement library for one shingle system family in one region; sign one founding sponsor under a written disclosure policy; recruit 300 contractors; run 500 jobs and measure supplement lift against matched jobs.

ideas.title: Pay-in-Five Managed Repair
ideas.one_liner: Managed repair priced on the days of displacement it removes, with contractors paid within five days of a verified milestone.
ideas.customer: Regional and mid-size homeowners carriers and residual-market plans with displaced households (fire, major water, smoke).
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Property Claims or Chief Claims Officer; a program fee from LAE plus a share of ALE (Coverage D) savings.
ideas.problem: ALE runs by the day (policies typically cap it around 20-30% of dwelling). California's AB 1795 now bars ending ALE before a home is remediated and safe. DRP networks are paid per assignment or by contractor referral fees, not for days saved, and contractors wait 60-90 days, which slows the job.
ideas.solution: Dispatch vetted contractors, pre-agree scope and price menus, run the project clock (permit, materials, trades), pay contractors in five days from escrow and the platform's balance sheet, and price against ALE-days saved versus a matched cohort.
ideas.why_now: AB 1795; claim volume down 20% pushes carriers to outcome-priced vendors; Crawford's network shows about $3B a year of managed-repair demand (company figure); Alacrity's managed-repair unit changed owners in Jan 2026.
ideas.wedge: Water and smoke losses (short scope, fast cycle) in TX and CA with two regional carriers and 40 contractors; first 10 customers are two carriers plus eight PE-backed restoration firms.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $3.3B of managed volume at a 3% fee is $100M: roughly 4% of the $82B pool and about Crawford Contractor Connection's present scale. Gain-share on top: ALE is perhaps 6-9% of indemnity, $5-7B (my assumption, no source found), so 20% of days saved at a 25% share is a $250-350M pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Crawford Contractor Connection (5,500 contractors, ~500k assignments), Altimeter Solutions Group (ex-Alacrity), HOMEE (AI DRP, W.R. Berkley-led Series C), Sedgwick, ServPro/Belfor programs, carriers' own DRPs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Referral and assignment fees pay them for volume, not speed, and they cannot fund fast pay; carriers cannot run contractor cash; contractors cannot carry 60-90 days. Counter-positioning: we give up referral fees and charge for days saved.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (TPAs would have to give up referral fees) plus switching costs from carrier integration.
ideas.earned_secret: Nobody owns the repair clock. ALE is paid on receipts by adjusters, while the days between loss and first trade on site, and between completion and final payment, belong to no one and are not measured.
ideas.first_90_days: Pitch three regional carriers and one residual-market plan on a 100-claim pilot of water and smoke losses with a matched control; pre-load 30 vetted contractors with five-day pay; measure ALE-days to first trade on site and to final payment.

ideas.title: Claims Escrow Co.
ideas.one_liner: The title company for insurance repair money: a licensed, bonded escrow that holds and releases claim proceeds against milestones and signs an indemnity to the servicer and carrier.
ideas.customer: Mortgage servicers and sub-servicers (loss-draft and compliance teams) and homeowners carriers; contractors and homeowners are the beneficiaries.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Servicers: SVP Servicing or head of loss draft plus the chief compliance officer. Carriers: VP Claims Ops. Budget lines are servicing operations, compliance and (for carriers) ALE; revenue is a draw fee, a share of float and an indemnity premium.
ideas.problem: About 61% of owner-occupied homes carry a mortgage. Carriers fear double indemnity if they bypass the mortgagee; servicers fear misapplied funds, now owe at least 2% interest on held proceeds in California (AB 493), and face a 10-business-day benchmark and a data order due 29 Oct 2026; manual first draws meet SLA only 22% of the time (vendor claim).
ideas.solution: A state-licensed escrow/trust company with bonded, insured custody. Proceeds go into a claim escrow; servicers code release rules; funds go out against milestones to contractors, suppliers (materials first, with lien waivers) and homeowners. A claim protection letter, like title's closing protection letter and backed by a surety or insurer, indemnifies servicer and carrier.
ideas.why_now: AB 493, the July 2026 governor's letters, the 15 Oct 2026 lender reporting order, AB 1842 and MA/HI bills turned custody from free float into a regulated liability, while Fannie Mae's current guide already lets servicers release up to the greatest of $40k, 33% or the excess over the loan balance up front.
ideas.wedge: California large-loss and total-loss claims at one top-25 servicer or sub-servicer plus the FAIR Plan or a California carrier, 100 files first.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: loss-draft-sized proceeds about $30B of the ~$50B mortgage-linked. A 0.4% draw fee is $120M and net float ($30B x 75/365 x 2%) is $123M, so about $243M at 100% share; adding contractor-payment protection on the ~$32B non-mortgaged dollars at 0.4% brings the pool to about $370M. $100M is 27-40% of the pool, so this is heroic: utility or nothing. Title (a few underwriters) and CCC in auto claims (~$1B revenue, unverified) show such networks concentrate.
ideas.who_does_it_today: iink ($2.5B+ processed, vendor claim), sureti/Checkbook ($3.25M raised, lenderless settlement), One Inc ClaimsPay (carrier-side payments), lender construction-draw software (e.g. Built, unverified), servicers in-house. No title or escrow company handles claim proceeds (none found).
ideas.why_they_lose: Each is one-sided: iink is a servicer deposit tool, sureti bypasses lenders without their consent, One Inc pays but does not hold funds against milestones. None issues a protection letter or carries a neutral fiduciary role.
ideas.moat: Network economies and switching costs, with a state licensing barrier.
ideas.earned_secret: Servicer ops managers will never speed up on their own, because every fast release is personal liability, but they will outsource to a party that signs an indemnity. And loss-draft float stopped being free once California mandated interest.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick the charter route (California escrow license plus a partner bank and a surety); sign one sub-servicer for a 100-file California pilot with its release rules coded; produce an AB 493-style interest and days-to-release report.

ideas.title: Mid-Band Advocate
ideas.one_liner: A licensed, software-run public adjuster for the $5-25k claims no public adjuster will take.
ideas.customer: Homeowners with $5-25k wind, hail and water claims, about 55% of claims or 1.9-2.4M a year (my assumption).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The homeowner pays an 8-10% contingent fee on the settlement, within state caps (TX 10%, FL 10%/20%), out of claim proceeds; signer is the homeowner.
ideas.problem: Public-adjuster economics fail below roughly $25k on acquisition cost and adjuster hours; contractors may not negotiate coverage in places like TX and FL; lawyers will not take small cases; carriers are the adverse party. The first offer becomes the settlement, and ACV schedules and carrier scrutiny widen the gap.
ideas.solution: Licensed in all 50 states (acquire small PA firms for licenses). Software reads the policy, estimate and photos, finds formulaic entitlements (overhead and profit, matching, code upgrade, labor depreciation, ALE, contents), drafts the presentation, and a licensed adjuster signs.
ideas.why_now: ACV roof schedules cut payouts, carriers are deploying AI to estimate and trim, claim volume down 20% raised scrutiny, and LLMs can now read policies cheaply.
ideas.wedge: TX and FL hail and wind roofs, reaching homeowners through contractors who adopt a free scope tool (Storm Pro Co-op) with no referral fees; first 10 customers are homeowners after a denial or low offer.
ideas.path_to_100m: 100k signed claims a year at about $1,200 is $120M, about 4-5% of the mid-band and 2.5-3% of all claims (my arithmetic from 3.5-4.3M claims). The binding constraint is customer acquisition cost, not market size.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Thousands of PA firms (fees 5-20%), consumer claim law firms, claim-fee advance funders (National Claims Funding), United Policyholders. No funded policyholder-side AI PA turned up in a single search, which is not conclusive.
ideas.why_they_lose: Hourly or relationship-based PAs cannot get to one hour per claim; contractors are legally barred from negotiating; carriers cannot advocate; lawyers cannot take small cases.
ideas.moat: Process power plus cornered resource (claims outcome data) and scale in multi-state licensing.
ideas.earned_secret: The missing dollars in mid-band claims are formulaic, roughly $1-4k each (unverified insider hypothesis). The economics break on adjuster time, not fee: six hours per claim fails, one hour works.
ideas.first_90_days: License in TX, FL, CO and CA; build the entitlement checker on 500 historic mid-band files; run 100 claims at an 8% fee cap and measure uplift over the first offer.

ideas.title: Fire and Smoke Program
ideas.one_liner: The clearance authority and program manager for smoke, soot, lead and asbestos claims, built on California's new AB 1642 / AB 1795 standards.
ideas.customer: Homeowners carriers and the California FAIR Plan, later all fire claims nationally.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of property claims at an LA-exposed carrier or the FAIR Plan; budget is Coverage A/C indemnity (testing, remediation) and ALE, paid as a program fee per file.
ideas.problem: About 13,000 of roughly 40,000 LA-fire claims are smoke damage to homes that did not burn. AB 1642 sets the first enforceable lead and asbestos testing and remediation standards; AB 1795 requires insurers to pay testing, remediation and full cleanup and bars cutting ALE until the home is remediated and safe. Insurers were reported to be stalling contamination claims a year on, and LA County sued State Farm.
ideas.solution: One program: intake, protocol sampling by accredited assessors (a network of industrial hygienists and lead/asbestos consultants), lab results, remediation scope at pre-agreed prices through vetted contractors with five-day pay, independent clearance test, and a clearance certificate that ends ALE and releases funds.
ideas.why_now: Signed 15 Sep 2026 (effective date not confirmed); ALE meters are running on thousands of files; no actor owns clearance end to end.
ideas.wedge: 200 LA smoke files from the FAIR Plan or a regional carrier; first 10 customers are three carriers plus seven remediation contractors and IH firms.
ideas.path_to_100m: LA alone: 13,000 files at about $6.5k ($4k testing and clearance plus 10% of $25k remediation, my assumptions) is about $85M over two years, maybe half capturable. National: fire is 21.6% of $82B = $17.7B (if the ISO share is by dollars); smoke, soot and contamination on non-total fires about 30-35% = $5-6B; an 8-9% fee is $450-540M, so $100M is about 20% and depends on other wildfire states copying the standard (unverified).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Restoration contractors that clear their own work (Belfor, ServPro), industrial-hygiene firms and labs, TPAs, DTSC guidance.
ideas.why_they_lose: Contractors cannot certify their own work, labs have no program or payment control, and carriers and TPAs gain from delay. Nobody owns the end-to-end clearance outcome.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (accredited experts and lab throughput) plus standard-setting.
ideas.earned_secret: Under AB 1795 the clearance test is what stops the ALE meter, so the result is worth thousands of dollars a month to the carrier, and each side distrusts the other's lab. A neutral clearance authority is worth more than the testing itself.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit 10 assessors and two labs in LA; write the clearance protocol to AB 1642 with a toxicologist; clear 100 homes and report ALE-days saved against matched files.

ideas.title: Certified Complete
ideas.one_liner: A neutral completion grade that releases the next loss-draft installment and ends the holdback and ALE clock.
ideas.customer: Servicer and sub-servicer loss-draft teams and carrier property claims; later underwriters, lenders and buyers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Servicer EVP Servicing Ops or head of loss draft (inspection vendor budget); carrier VP Property Claims (reinspection and holdback release).
ideas.problem: Remaining funds follow periodic inspections under Fannie Mae's guide; manual first draws meet SLA only 22% of the time (vendor claim). Every party to 'done' is conflicted: contractor wants paid, carrier wants to stop ALE and the holdback, homeowner wants the cash, servicer wants no liability.
ideas.solution: A third-party grade built from device-attested milestone capture (tear-off, dry-in, rough-in, final), permit finals, lien waivers and a license check, with risk-based sampling by licensed inspectors and a bonded guarantee behind the grade. The servicer codes its policy ('release on grade X'); carriers accept the grade for holdback and ALE.
ideas.why_now: California's 10-business-day benchmark, 29 Oct 2026 reporting order and AB 493 interest put servicers under a clock; AB 1795 makes clearance legally meaningful; Fannie Mae's current guide gives servicers room to release more up front if they have evidence; AI-doctored images push toward attested capture (unverified).
ideas.wedge: A 60-day shadow pilot on 200 open California loss drafts at one sub-servicer, then one top-10 carrier on holdback release.
ideas.path_to_100m: My arithmetic: servicer files about 1.2M (4M claims x 60.7% x about half above the loss-draft threshold) x 2.2 inspections x $90 = $240M; carrier holdback and final reinspection 0.8M x $75 = $60M; clearance and post-remediation testing 600k x $350 = $210M (overlaps the Fire and Smoke idea); repair-history lookups 20M x $1 = $20M. Pool about $530M, so $100M is about 19%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Servicers' in-house teams and field-inspection vendors, iink (digital loss draft), capture apps (Encircle, CompanyCam, Hover), industrial-hygiene labs, carrier reinspection staff.
ideas.why_they_lose: Inspectors are paid per visit, so they have no reason to remove visits; capture apps are tools, not accepted standards; contractors cannot self-certify; carriers are conflicted. A grader both sides accept is a chokepoint, as PSA is for trading cards.
ideas.moat: Network economies and standard (once servicers and carriers codify the grade as the release trigger, contractors must produce it) plus cornered resource (verification outcomes become a repair-history asset).
ideas.earned_secret: Servicers inspect not because rules require it (Fannie's current text lets them release a large first draw and skip a final inspection on current loans) but because no one will vouch for the contractor. The fear is liens and unfinished work, not workmanship, so a lien waiver, permit final and license check plus a party that stands behind the grade removes most visits.
ideas.first_90_days: Shadow-grade 200 open California loss drafts and compare to what the servicer released and inspected; if the grade predicts every decision, convert to a per-draw fee that replaces inspections; get one top-10 carrier to accept the certificate for holdback or ALE release on 100 claims.

ideas.title: Coverage Continuity Desk: servicer-paid, borrower-aligned replacement for lender-placed tracking
ideas.one_liner: Charge mortgage servicers a flat per-loan fee to keep every escrowed borrower's policy alive and cure non-renewals before force-placement, replacing 'free' tracking that is funded by lender-placed premium.
ideas.customer: Servicing operations at the largest mortgage servicers. First 10: three mid-size nonbank servicers (0.5-3M loans) with heavy CA, FL, TX, CO books, reached through MBA servicing forums and compliance heads who already field force-placement complaints.
ideas.payer_and_signer: SVP Servicing Operations (insurance, escrow, hazard loss), with the Chief Compliance Officer co-signing for Reg X force-placed rules. Budget lines: escrow and loss-draft processing (MBA: $11 a loan, sourced), complaint handling and default-servicing cost. Fee (assumed): $6 a loan a year.
ideas.problem: A servicer sees the premium jump, the non-renewal notice and the lapse before the borrower acts, but routes the case to a tracking vendor whose economics run on lender-placed insurance. Assurant tracks 34M+ loans and places about 2% (Q2 2026, sourced); NAIC calls LPI a 'reverse competition' market because the payer is not the chooser. Every cure is revenue the tracker loses. Servicers cannot shop for borrowers or earn a commission without RESPA exposure (hazard insurance is a settlement service), so nobody is paid to keep the borrower on a normal policy. About 2.03M homeowners policies were non-renewed in 2024 (derived from NAIC regional data), up 96-216% since 2018.
ideas.solution: Fee-for-service with no commissions: (1) evidence matching so borrowers who renewed under a new policy number or agent are not force-placed; (2) outreach inside the non-renewal period rather than the 45-day force-place window; (3) placement through a licensed partner with the servicer receiving nothing per policy; (4) premium-shock and escrow-shortage calls; (5) carrier-insolvency playbook; (6) mortgagee-clause re-papering after servicing transfers. Legal premise to check: RESPA Section 8 / 12 CFR 1024.15 (payment only for services actually performed), Reg X 1024.37 notice timing, state licensing for the placement partner.
ideas.why_now: FAIR Plan +29.1% on Oct 15 2026; State Farm's no-nonrenewal stay ends Dec 31 2026 (news summary); California DFPI is now reading servicer behaviour (Oct 15 order); Rocket must pick one insurance stack for about 10M loans after the Mr. Cooper merger, a rare buying event (my inference); Assurant is still adding clients (Freedom Mortgage, Q2 2026), so the incumbent is entrenched but visibly dependent on LPI growth.
ideas.wedge: One mid-size servicer's CA/FL/TX non-renewal cohort: contact within 10 days of the carrier letter, then report borrowers kept on voluntary coverage and LPI placements avoided.
ideas.path_to_100m: Four to five servicers with about 18M loans (Rocket/Mr. Cooper about 10M, sourced; two or three others at 2-4M, assumed) x $6 a loan = $108M. By loan count that is about 30% of roughly 60M first liens (derived from Rocket's '1 in 6 mortgages'), which is heroic as a share, but it needs only four or five signatures. The fee sits below the $11 a loan MBA line it substitutes for. Unverified: whether servicers will pay an explicit fee when tracking is currently funded by LPI.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Assurant (tracking and LPI), National General/Allstate (TrackGuard LPI claims), ICE/Black Knight insurance services (unverified), Matic (embedded shopping, about $99M raised, 100+ distribution partners, commission model), Hippo-style servicer partnerships, in-house hazard-loss teams.
ideas.why_they_lose: Assurant cannot cut LPI without cutting its own profit pool (non-cat loss ratio about 35%). Matic is paid by carriers per bound policy, so it cannot be the servicer's neutral compliance operator and it raises the RESPA referral question. In-house teams are cost centres with no data on outcomes after a cure.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against the LPI-funded tracker, plus switching costs from servicing-platform integration (12-18 month conversions) and process power from a cure-rate dataset.
ideas.earned_secret: The valuable window is the weeks between a non-renewal letter and the lapse, while the borrower still has an agent and a carrier will still quote; after force-placement the borrower is on E&S or FAIR at 2-3x the price and the servicer has a complaint. Also, a share of 'lapses' are matching failures, not real lapses (insider hypothesis, unverified; validate on ten servicers' LPI refund reports).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one pilot servicer; ingest 12 months of LPI placements and refunds to quantify erroneous placements; run outreach on 5,000 non-renewal cases; get a written RESPA/Reg X memo for the placement-partner structure.

ideas.title: Placement Desk: pay for the agent's hour (distressed-risk exchange for FAIR, E&S and take-out carriers)
ideas.one_liner: An exchange where an agent submits a distressed home once, the declinations are documented, and the home is quoted and bound across FAIR, E&S and take-out carriers, because the shortage in this market is agent minutes, not capacity.
ideas.customer: Independent agencies holding distressed books (CA first, then FL, TX, CO), plus the carriers that want that volume. First 10: 15 California agencies with 100+ FAIR policies each; three admitted carriers with SIS writing commitments; three E&S MGAs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Carriers pay a bind fee or wholesale split (signer: VP Distribution; budget: new-business acquisition, 12-15% commission plus marketing). Agencies pay a seat (assumed $300-500 a month). The FAIR Plan pays nothing.
ideas.problem: Insider estimate (unverified): a distressed submission takes 2-4 hours across 6-10 portals. FAIR averages about $2,930 a policy ($1.96B / 668,609), so a 7% new commission is about $205 and a 3% renewal about $88 (rates sourced from Insurance Journal, scope by line unconfirmed). At $50-70 an hour loaded cost, renewals are underwater and new business is break-even, so agents drop service and policyholders orphan. Carriers with appetite cannot reach agents' attention; the FAIR Clearinghouse works only through the broker of record (unverified commercial guide).
ideas.solution: One ACORD-plus-photos-plus-mitigation-evidence packet; automatic California diligent-search/declination documentation for E&S; appetite matching; parallel quote and bind by API or portal automation; the agent keeps the retail commission, the desk takes the wholesale split or bind fee; renewal servicing for orphaned FAIR policies at near-zero marginal cost. Legal premise to check: surplus-lines broker licensing and the diligent-search rule, FAIR producer rules, BOR letters.
ideas.why_now: FAIR +29.1% and the commission cuts start Oct 15 2026; E&S homeowners premium +29.5% to $4.14B in 2025 and California surplus-lines policies passed 300,000, about 90% urban, so as SIS rates become adequate those good homes can flow back to admitted carriers; Citizens fell to 266,093 so Florida carriers want growth; cat reinsurance pricing is down 15-25%; State Farm's stay ends Dec 31 2026.
ideas.wedge: FAIR-to-admitted take-outs and E&S placements for 15 agencies; prove 300 binds, then add Florida and Texas carriers.
ideas.path_to_100m: E&S homeowners $4.14B growing 15% a year (assumed) is about $6.3B in 2029; a 6% wholesale/bind take is about $378M. Add 144k FAIR exits a year (24k in two months, annualised) x $450 desk revenue = $65M, and orphan servicing about $12M. Pool about $455M, so $100M is about 22% of it. Heroic; at 10% share the desk earns about $45M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Bridge Specialty (digital personal-lines marketplace launched April 2026), CRC, Amwins, RT Specialty, Burns & Wilcox, Young Alfred/Credible ($10M Series A), Novella and Pathpoint (commercial only), Matic (origination), Kin/Openly/Slide (carriers), the California FAIR Clearinghouse (about 15 carriers).
ideas.why_they_lose: Wholesalers' cost structures assume $5k+ commercial premiums; FAIR cannot market; D2C aggregators earn per lead and have no hard-risk carriers; carriers' captive channels cannot use an agent exchange.
ideas.moat: Network economies (agents and carriers) and process power from portal automation; main threat is Applied/Vertafore/EZLynx bundling a rater (race-the-bundle).
ideas.earned_secret: Agents are not refusing distressed risks because markets are closed; they refuse because the hours do not pay. Paying the agent's time with carrier-funded bind fees frees more capacity than any new carrier (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 15 agencies and six carriers; automate five portals; run 300 submissions and publish minutes-per-bind and bind rate.

ideas.title: Proceeds Desk: custody, draws and contractor fast-pay for insurance money
ideas.one_liner: Take the monitored loss-draft file off the servicer: hold proceeds in a bank-partner account, release by machine-checked milestones, and pay contractors in two days for a small fee.
ideas.customer: Servicers and depository lenders holding insurance proceeds. First 10: California credit unions and community banks with LA-fire loans (they owe DFPI a report by about Oct 29 2026) plus two nonbank servicers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of Loss Draft / Hazard Loss (signer: SVP Servicing Operations, with the Chief Compliance Officer) from the loss-draft processing line ($11 a loan, MBA) and compliance remediation. Contractors pay the fast-pay fee; insurers can pay per evidence packet for RC-holdback releases.
ideas.problem: Proceeds are payable jointly to borrower and servicer; large claims are 'monitored' (RoundPoint: above $40k or delinquent) and released in thirds after inspections by a roughly $100 third-party inspector who cannot read a schedule, while the contractor cannot start without money.
