California now has AB 493 (interest on held proceeds), a July 2026 order on holds over 10 days and an Oct 15 2026 reporting order; DFPI has 160+ complaints; 16,000+ structures were destroyed and fewer than a dozen rebuilt one year on. Disputes over percent complete are the stated cause.
ideas.solution: (1) Digital multi-party endorsement; (2) a custodial FBO account per claim at a partner bank, interest passed through; (3) release rules encoded from the servicer's policy and checked against permit-status feeds, dated geotagged photos, contractor licence and insurance, and statutory lien waivers; (4) contractor fast-pay on approved draws at 1-2% (assumed); (5) later, a completion guaranty and a soft-cost bridge secured on the proceeds. Legal premise to check: money transmission (use a bank partner), security-instrument terms (restore if feasible), state inspection-before-release rules, California lien-waiver forms.
ideas.why_now: Oct 15 2026 DFPI order, AB 493, hurricane Isaias (Oct 10, $2.5-4.5B insured), and the March 2026 GSE letter accepting ACV roofs, which widens depreciation gaps on hail claims.
ideas.wedge: California fire loan books: median days from check receipt to homeowner disbursement under 10, with an interest ledger and a DFPI-ready export; then monitored claims nationally.
ideas.path_to_100m: Direct losses about $102B (61.59% of $165.2B) x 60% mortgaged x 50% monitored (assumed) = $30.5B of proceeds a year (if monitored is 30%, the pool falls to about $340M). Servicer fee: about 305k files x $600 = $183M. Contractor fast-pay: $21B of draws x 1.5% = $320M. Float spread 0.5% on about $12.7B average balance = $64M. Pool about $567M; add a completion guaranty (about $80M) and bridge interest (about $100M) for about $750M. $100M is 13-18% blended share. Heroic, but three payers stack.
ideas.who_does_it_today: iink (check capture and multi-party payments; $14.8M raised; self-reports 162,029 claims and $2.3B of proceeds), DIMONT (loss-draft service), National General/Assurant LPI claims, servicers' own loss-draft teams, The Hub/CORE (nonprofit escrow oversight in LA), Built Technologies and title-company disbursers (construction lending, not insurance money).
ideas.why_they_lose: iink moves checks but does not decide releases, has no contractor credit and is small. Servicers cannot underwrite contractors or hold interest-bearing accounts cheaply under AB 493. The Hub is local and philanthropic.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (servicer integrations, DFPI audit trail) and process power; contractor draw history becomes credit data (cornered resource).
ideas.earned_secret: The money is not slow because servicers are lazy; it is deadlocked: the inspector's percent-complete is a judgment call and nobody will pre-fund the contractor. Replace the judgment with evidence and release becomes mechanical. Outside California servicers also earn float on these balances, so expect resistance until other states copy AB 493 (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign two CA lenders with open fire files; process 200 draws at cost; connect LA County permit data; sign one bank partner; agree fast-pay terms with 20 rebuild contractors.

ideas.title: Closing Desk: outcome-priced total-loss claim operation with a regulatory warranty
ideas.one_liner: Take a carrier's major-loss and total-loss files end to end (contents, ALE, debris, dwelling scope, mortgagee) for a fixed fee per closed file, with a cap-limited warranty on statutory clocks.
ideas.customer: VP Property Claims at mid-size carriers, reciprocals, Florida domestics and residual plans. First 10: 100 open LA total-loss files at a mid-size carrier or the FAIR Plan; a Florida domestic after Isaias.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Claims Officer from the outsourced LAE budget (adjusting and TPA fees); the compliance officer co-signs because the warranty reduces exam exposure.
ideas.problem: Total losses run as separate queues (dwelling, contents, ALE, debris, mortgagee), each with a different adjuster; reassignment resets clocks. CDI listed repeated adjuster reassignment, late status letters and underpayments among 398 violations in a 220-file sample of State Farm; penalties are small ($10,000 per willful violation) but a one-year licence suspension is sought. State Farm is about 78% closed after roughly 20 months. SB 495 (effective Jan 1 2026) requires a 60% contents advance without inventory in declared emergencies.
ideas.solution: One case owner per file, a clock engine for every statutory deadline, templates for status and ALE-extension letters, SB 495 advance workflow, contents valuation, vendor routing, and an indemnity for penalties up to a cap. Surge mode with pre-credentialed adjusters on retainer. Priced per closed file with a cycle-time bonus.
ideas.why_now: CDI Accusation (May 4 2026), LA County suit (Aug 31 2026), ALE ends Jan 7 2027 for many survivors, and the Sept 2026 mitigation rule add clocks; State Farm's closure rate gives every carrier a public benchmark.
ideas.wedge: Contents plus ALE workflow on open Palisades/Eaton files, priced per closed file.
ideas.path_to_100m: Outsourced adjusting about $11.7B (IBISWorld, all lines) x 35% property (assumed) = $4.1B; x 40% major/cat/total-loss (assumed) = $1.6B; $100M is about 6%. Cross-check: about 150k major-loss files a year (assumed) x $6,000 = $900M; $100M is about 11%. No homeowners LAE ratio was found, so these shares are assumptions.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sedgwick (property split into five product lines, desk outsourcing accepted), Crawford ($1.27B 2025 revenue), Pilot, Frontline, Engle Martin, Alacrity; policyholder-side Claim Architect; AI newcomers (Curant.ai $3.1M seed, Sprout.ai); carriers' own major-loss units.
ideas.why_they_lose: IA firms bill by the hour or file, so automation shrinks their revenue; their adjusters are 1099s shared across firms; none sells a compliance warranty.
ideas.moat: Process power and switching costs (delegated authority, carrier-system integration); scale economies in surge capacity.
ideas.earned_secret: Total losses are slow because five queues restart each other, not because estimating is hard. One owner and a clock engine cut reassignments, and the warranty is only priceable once the clocks are automated (insider hypothesis, unverified). Cliche flag: 'AI claims' is on the cliche list; the differentiators are the warranty and total-loss scope, not first notice of loss.
ideas.first_90_days: Take 100 open files at fixed price; measure reassignments, days to ALE decision and days to contents payment; get an E&O carrier to quote the warranty.

ideas.title: Soft-Landing Exchange: outplacement for non-renewed policyholders, sold to the carrier that is leaving
ideas.one_liner: Sell the leaving carrier a consent-based service that moves its non-renewed policyholders to quoted, bindable offers from other carriers, and keep the resulting agent-of-record commission.
ideas.customer: Carriers cutting exposure in CA, FL, TX, CO and LA, and regulators who want softer exits. First 10: State Farm General's slated nonrenewals for 2027 (about 72,000 announced in 2024, unverified), plus Travelers, Chubb, Nationwide, USAA, Farmers and Allstate, all reported as having pulled back in high-risk California areas.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Exiting carrier (signer: VP Customer/Regulatory Affairs; budget: nonrenewal handling, call centre, complaint and regulatory-risk cost, assumed about $30 a policy); buyer carriers via commission (about 12% of premium, assumed).
ideas.problem: A non-renewal is legally a termination, not a referral. The captive agent cannot place elsewhere, the carrier cannot recommend a competitor, and the policyholder starts from zero inside roughly 75 days (unverified). About 2.03M policies a year are non-renewed; most dissolve into the market and the buyer carriers' acquisition value (about $500 a policy, assumed) is never captured.
ideas.solution: The notice carries an opt-in link; on consent the desk becomes agent of record, pre-qualifies the home against 5-10 appetites using the carrier's own data, shows bindable offers within 24 hours and handles BOR and mortgagee changes. The exiting carrier gets a regulator-ready harm-mitigation report. Legal premise to check: policyholder data-sharing consent (California Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act), nonrenewal notice content rules, any CDI view on carrier-paid referral services, agent licensing.
ideas.why_now: State Farm's no-nonrenewal stay ends Dec 31 2026; NAIC data show nonrenewals up 96-216% since 2018; CDI and the Governor are publicly measuring harm to homeowners; FAIR growth slowed to 1.9% as it tries to depopulate.
ideas.wedge: One carrier's 2027 slated cohort handled as a managed transfer; free pilot on 5,000 policies.
ideas.path_to_100m: 2.03M nonrenewals x 60% re-placeable (assumed) = 1.22M a year. At 15% share that is 183k placements a year; with 85% retention (assumed) the in-force book after five years is about 678k policies. At $2,400 premium x 12% commission x 70% after local-agent splits = $200 a policy, revenue is about $135M in year five. Needs about 15% of the flow; the exiting-carrier fee adds only about $5M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: No service sold to the exiting carrier was found. Adjacent: Policygenius, Insurify and The Zebra (leads), Matic (origination), Young Alfred, Bridge Specialty (agents), the FAIR Clearinghouse, retail agents.
ideas.why_they_lose: Aggregators are paid per lead by buyers and have no access to the exiting carrier's data or notice. Captive agents are contractually stuck. The FAIR Clearinghouse serves only FAIR policies.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (a service no carrier or aggregator can offer), cornered resource (carrier-originated cohorts) and recurring commission that accumulates.
ideas.earned_secret: Carriers lose more from the exit story than from the exit: complaints, legislators, press. They already pay for outplacement of laid-off employees; the same logic applies to customers (my inference, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Offer one carrier a free pilot on 5,000 non-renewed policies; measure rebind rate and time to bind; get an informal CDI view.

ideas.title: Draw and Price Oracle: the conflict-free percent-complete and paid-invoice price standard (weakest, flagged)
ideas.one_liner: A neutral percent-complete and paid-invoice price standard that servicers, insurers, contractors and appraisers can all accept, built as the data layer of the Proceeds Desk.
ideas.customer: Servicers (draw approvals), insurers (RC holdback and ALE evidence), public adjusters, contractors and appraisal umpires. First 10: the lenders from the Proceeds Desk plus two PA firms.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Servicer loss-draft head (inspection line), carrier property-claims VP (reserving and disputes), PA principal, litigation counsel.
ideas.problem: Xactimate's list is the de facto price standard, and contractors and advocates say it lags real costs after a surge (advocacy sources). Verisk sells to carriers and contractors and agreed to buy the roofer CRM AccuLynx for $2.35B; Delaware ordered it to perform on Aug 7 2026, and the FTC's reported theory is that Verisk could build an exclusive pricing integration that forecloses rivals. Nobody neutral can say what a line item cost or how complete a job is.
ideas.solution: Photo, permit and invoice ingestion scores percent complete and flags overbilling; a paid-invoice index by line item, ZIP and month; auditable evidence packets for supplements, RC-holdback releases and appraisals.
ideas.why_now: Verisk/AccuLynx ruling and FTC review; LA price disputes; reinsurers and regulators asking about demand surge.
ideas.wedge: Use the Proceeds Desk's draws as the data source; sell evidence packets to LA public adjusters.
ideas.path_to_100m: Servicer inspections: about 305k monitored files x 3 x $100 = $92M at 100% share. Contractor/PA seats: 100k x $600 = $60M. Carrier benchmark licences: 25 x $1M = $25M. Packets: about $15M. Pool about $190M, so $100M needs over 50% of it. It does not reach $100M alone; treat it as a data layer whose value shows up as higher release rates in the Proceeds Desk.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Verisk Xactware (Xactimate; Xactware says 22 of the top 25 US insurers use its tools), Symbility/Cotality, in-house price lists, expert witnesses.
ideas.why_they_lose: Verisk cannot publish a price that contradicts its own list or undercuts its carrier customers; Cotality has the same customer mix.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (paid-invoice data), but only if the Proceeds Desk wins first.
ideas.earned_secret: Disputes are rarely about the dollar amount of a line; they are about the date of the price and the percent complete. A dated paid-invoice index ends the argument (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Load 500 LA invoices; compare to the Xactimate list for the same month; publish the gap.

ideas.title: Rebuild Velocity: an insurer-paid owner's rep priced on ALE months saved
ideas.one_liner: A neutral, homeowner-trusted rebuild coordinator (permits, design, bids, code upgrades, draw readiness) paid a share of the ALE months it saves for the insurer carrying the meter.
ideas.customer: Carriers with open total-loss files in LA and later hurricane, tornado and hail total losses. First 10: three carriers with at least 100 open LA files, plus the FAIR Plan.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Property Claims (budget: ALE and indemnity), with servicers contributing for draw readiness and homeowners paying a small fee.
ideas.problem: The meter runs on the carrier: fewer than a dozen homes rebuilt one year on; 1,153 permits issued of about 2,900 applications by Jan 2 2026; ALE ends Jan 7 2027 for many survivors, extendable up to 12 months on reasonable diligence; NBC LA (July 2026) says 38% have run out or soon will; LA County's suit alleges ALE caps. Survivors are first-time builders; soft costs are $200k-350k+ before a shovel (marketing source, unverified); insurers cannot manage construction and servicers will not release money without progress.
ideas.solution: A neutral coordinator takes the homeowner from payout to permitted start, produces dated progress evidence that satisfies the 'reasonable diligence' test, and lines up draws with the servicer. Paid 40% of ALE months saved (ALE assumed at $5,000 a month; no ALE data found) plus a homeowner fee. Legal premise (decisive, unverified): whether an insurer paying this is steering, an inducement or unlicensed contracting under California rules; the cleanest structure is an opt-in benefit tied to ALE extension.
ideas.why_now: Jan 7 2027 ALE cliff, the LA County suit, and the state's focus on payouts; insurers face a 12-month extension liability on thousands of households.
ideas.wedge: 500 LA households with the longest-open ALE; guarantee four months saved or no fee.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 13,000 homes destroyed x 55% insured primary residences needing extension (assumed) = about 7,150; a 12-month extension at $5k a month is about $430M of insurer cost. Saving four months is $20k a household; at $10k revenue a household (insurer 40% share plus homeowner and servicer fees) LA is about $70M, spread over two to three years. Nationally about 60k major rebuilds a year (assumed) x $10k = $600M; $100M is about 17%. Heroic, and LA is a one-time pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Homebound (design-build with permitting and insurance advisors), The Hub/CORE (project management and escrow oversight), LA County One-Stop Permit Centers (free), Habitat plus Foothill Catalog (pre-approved plans), Samara/Steadfast and Cover (modular), Claim Architect (policyholder-side estimates), RockRose (mitigation). No insurer-funded programme was found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each is paid by the homeowner or by charity; none is paid by the party carrying the meter, and none is neutral enough to certify diligence.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (permit and contractor throughput data) and process power; weak until an insurer signs.
ideas.earned_secret: The biggest controllable cost in a total loss is time to rebuild, not the dwelling number, and nobody owns it; the insurer wants it owned but cannot own construction (insider hypothesis, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Offer three carriers a no-fee pilot on 100 files; measure months from payout to permit; get counsel's view on the payment structure.

ideas.title: Defensible-Space Network: annual, verified, route-dense fire-hardening subscription
ideas.one_liner: A route-dense subscription that keeps the 0-5 ft and 100 ft zones compliant every year and produces an inspection-grade record that insurers and fire departments accept.
ideas.customer: Homeowners in very high fire zones and state responsibility areas; HOAs; insurers that want fewer high-risk renewals. First 10: 500 homes in one local-responsibility-area city with an active fire-department inspection programme (LA County charges $151 a parcel).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Homeowner (subscription, assumed $1,000 a year); HOA board (signer: president or treasurer); insurers may co-fund for high-score policies (unverified, to be tested).
ideas.problem: The 100-ft defensible-space law has applied since 2005. Zone 0 emergency rules were adopted Aug 19 2026 for close to 2M homes, with existing-home deadlines of 3-5 years (earliest about 2029; sources conflict). CAL FIRE can fund only 129,206 inspections a year against a 250,000 goal. Insurers must credit mitigation and offer free inspections (CDI FAQ rev. Sep 4 2026). Compliance decays within a year and no one sells upkeep with proof.
ideas.solution: Annual or quarterly crews, goats and chippers on routes, with before-and-after geotagged evidence stored for the fire department and insurers; certificate packet for sale and rating credits; add Zone 0 conversions when deadlines bite.
ideas.why_now: Zone 0 adoption, the Sept 4 CDI FAQ, the inspection capacity gap, and unfunded state loans (SB 894 signed Sep 29 2026 with no appropriation) mean homeowners pay and need proof.
ideas.wedge: One city, 500 homes, a letter from the fire department accepting the evidence format.
ideas.path_to_100m: 100,000 homes x $1,000 a year = $100M, which is 5% of the roughly 2M Zone 0 homes (assumed price and uptake). Needs multi-state expansion for safety. Zone 0 retrofit spend is upside, not the base case.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Local tree and landscape firms (thousands), goat grazers, RockRose (roll-up of tree-trimming and roofing firms; $12.5M Series A; considering a $30-40M credit facility), BurnBot (Mercury-backed), private fire-defence contractors hired by insurers (unverified), Fire Safe Councils, CAL FIRE and local fire departments.
ideas.why_they_lose: Local firms cannot document to an insurer's standard or build routes across towns. RockRose is a carrier/broker first and early.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (route density), switching costs (the compliance record) and a possible standard if fire departments accept the evidence format.
ideas.earned_secret: Compliance is an annual re-grow problem, not a one-time retrofit, so it is a subscription; a homeowner who clears once drifts out of compliance within 12 months (insider hypothesis, unverified). Whiplash flag: Zone 0 existing-home deadlines may slip, so the business should stand on the 2005 law and insurer credits first.
ideas.first_90_days: Agree the evidence format with a fire department; run 100 homes; test whether two insurers will credit or co-pay; price at $75-100 a month.

verdicts.title: Custody Mutual: jail-health liability program priced on clinical process data

competitors_found.name: County risk pools (e.g. Association of County Commissioners of Oklahoma pools)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pool jail and law-enforcement liability for member counties; created because commercial cover was unavailable
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Cover most Oklahoma county jails; pool-level premiums in the hundreds of thousands per county

competitors_found.name: Correctional Risk Services (via Montana Association of Counties)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Administers catastrophic inmate medical insurance and claims administration programs for state county associations

competitors_found.name: E&S jail insurance wholesalers (Complete Markets storefront)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Place jail liability, professional liability and excess limits for counties and private jails in the surplus-lines market
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Mature brokerage channel; no funded jail-specific insurtech found

competitors_found.name: Maine statutory county jail-medical pool
competitors_found.what_they_do: State law lets 5+ counties self-fund a pool covering 80% of jail medical expenses over $10,000 per prisoner

verdicts.substitutes: Taxpayer self-insurance (Multnomah-style self-funding), county pools and joint-powers authorities, vendor-purchased professional liability with the county as additional insured, higher deductibles (Rockingham NC deductible rose from $10k to $200k), and counties simply dropping or reducing limits.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Idea assumes 1,200 deaths x 30-40% claim rate x $2-3M = $0.7-1.4B. Observed settlements are lower and selection-biased (Cuyahoga $1.35M across 4 suits, San Bernardino $3.23M across 4; the $9-20M cases are the news). At about $0.75M per claim the loss pool is nearer $0.5B, premium-equivalent about $0.7B, insurable share about $0.3-0.4B. Real whole-package county premiums are $0.35M (Rockingham NC) to $0.7M (Camden GA). $100M GWP is 25-30% share, and an MGA keeps only about 15-20% of it, so $100M GWP is about $15-20M revenue. Booking $100M of revenue means becoming the risk-bearing carrier (about $60-70M surplus, long-tail reserving).
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Vendors hand over EHR timestamps despite discovery risk: low plausibility. (2) Process indicators actually separate bad from average outcomes in 50 closed claims: unknown but cheap to test. (3) A fronting carrier and reinsurer back a first-of-kind program: plausible. (4) 15-20% share of insurable jail liability in 6 years via pools: low-to-moderate. Reaching $100M of revenue additionally requires converting to a risk-bearing carrier with 25-30% share: not credible.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: PSQIA protects only patient safety work product reported to a PSO, never original medical records; in Crawford v. Corizon (jail death) the court ordered most documents produced because the vendor could not show they were assembled for a PSO. I found nothing on whether sharing with a liability insurer waives privilege. Deliberate indifference turns on what officials knew, so a dashboard showing notice creates the exhibit it claims to prevent. Punitive damages are barred against counties under Newport v. Fact Concerts (background knowledge), so that gate is narrower than the idea says. The Wellpath indemnity-gap premise is real (self-insured retentions up to $8M per incident, Cobb County fraud suit) but the cover counties actually need is mostly bought via additional-insured status, not a new MGA.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Insurable pool is about $0.3-0.4B; $100M GWP is 25-30% share and only about $15-20M of MGA revenue; the data and privilege premises are fragile.

verdicts.title: Outside Care Plan: the DOC's own off-site health plan

competitors_found.name: Prime Health Services / Prime Corrections
competitors_found.what_they_do: Savings-share bill review and repricing of off-site inmate medical bills for county sheriffs (NC sheriffs plan since 2011, Florida, Wisconsin); no risk, no access guarantees
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Flagler County alone saved $1.05M in a year; idea cites $88M cumulative documented savings

competitors_found.name: Heritage Health Care Solutions (Polk County FL TPA sole-source)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Third-party administrator adjudicating and paying off-site inmate medical and pharmacy claims for a county

competitors_found.name: Centene / Centurion
competitors_found.what_they_do: Medicaid-plan parent running full-service state prison health contracts, incl. hospital networks and risk (Maryland $1.7B prisons plus $723M pretrial)

competitors_found.name: CDCR/CCHCS provider network and prior authorization (RFP SD25-00019)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Largest state's off-site specialty network and prior authorization procured as a TPA-style contract
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Five-year term plus five one-year extensions; value not stated

competitors_found.name: State university and state-paid models (Texas, Iowa, Connecticut, Georgia, NC corrections hospitals)
competitors_found.what_they_do: 17 states deliver care directly and 4 use a university model; they pay off-site claims from their own budget, usually at Medicaid or Medicare-based schedules

verdicts.substitutes: State-set fee schedules (Mississippi 200% of Medicaid; South Carolina 135% of Medicare; Utah and NC lower rates for non-contract hospitals; California receiver caps), Medicaid inpatient claiming for expansion-state stays, carve-out of inpatient care in 5 states, repricing TPAs, and the state simply replacing the failed vendor (Alabama to NaphCare, Maryland to Centurion).
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Off-site is 20-27% of about $11B = $2.2-3.0B headline (Pew confirms 27% Virginia, 23% New York). But Pew shows Medicaid expansion moved most inpatient stays to Medicaid at the lowest rates, 5 states already carve out inpatient care, and 17 states plus 4 university-model states already pay off-site directly. My haircut: about $1.4-2.0B reachable. As a risk-bearer revenue is premium, so $100M is about 5-7% of that (one large state or 2-3 mid-size), at 5-8% margin = $5-8M gross profit. Prime's $88M in cumulative savings over about 14 years shows the non-risk repricing fee pool is tiny.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) 2-3 states restructure a vendor or in-house arrangement to carve hospital payments out to a third-party risk-bearer: no 2026 precedent (every shock produced a vendor swap), low plausibility. (2) Hospitals accept Medicare-plus rates for 15-day payment and 5-10 year volume: plausible. (3) Insurer or health-plan licensure and stop-loss are workable in target states: unknown, unverified. (4) Georgia-style unpaid-provider fallout makes a 'payer of last resort' valuable to DOCs: plausible but not yet a procurement trend.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Assuming risk for hospital claims on a prepaid basis likely triggers insurance or HMO licensure in many states; not verified per state. Federal precedent (Marshals/BOP Medicare-based pricing) is real but state rate caps already capture much of the repricing. HHS-OIG is auditing improper Medicaid capitation payments for incarcerated people (report due 2026), a regulatory flag for the Medicaid-match piece.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Real budget line and pain, but states already hold carve-outs, Medicaid rates and TPAs, 2026 buyers replaced vendors instead of restructuring, and risk-bearing needs licensure and capital for a 5-8% margin.

Wrong-payer risk is real (Connecticut study put savings in the justice budget). Federal Medicaid cuts and work requirements from 2027 are a flagged risk.

(3) Win 300-400 Texas full-service beds plus 150-200 in Washington/Oklahoma/other states over 5-6 years: plausible for top-decile execution. (4) Licensure and psychiatric/RN staffing hold up on a 6-12 month timeline: moderate. (5) Incumbents with owned beds do not win everything: moderate.

No. 1:16-CV-00917, Judge Ezra, permanent injunction 2026-07-07, 21 days from commitment order, four years to comply, state asked the Fifth Circuit to postpone benchmarks and argues the remedy was never constitutionally required (no ruling found).
