picks.from_title: Day 21: forensic capacity for court-ordered competency restoration
picks.title: Day 21: multi-state operator of full-service forensic restoration beds
picks.one_liner: An operator that adds licensed secure forensic beds in 6-12 months, paid per available bed-day by state forensic agencies under court deadlines, starting with Texas.
picks.sharpened_pitch: A multi-state operator of full-service secure competency-restoration beds, sold on 5-year availability-based contracts to state forensic agencies, delivered in leased and modular licensed units next to existing campuses, with an owned clinical staffing pool and an outpatient restoration track for low-risk defendants. Do not make jail-hosted treatment-only slots the core: Liberty's San Bernardino contract works out to about $170 per bed-day (county supplies the bed) and Harris County's program about $261, while full-service beds price at $412-$800 and Wellpath Recovery Solutions earns about $388 per patient-day. $100M needs about 600 full-service beds at $450. Texas is the anchor: the wait list was 1,626 in June 2026, HHSC adds only 175 net new beds by 2027 and told lawmakers it will still be short, and a state-built bed costs about $3.7M against about $164k a year for a contracted one. Then replicate under the same kind of pressure in Washington, Oklahoma and Colorado. Use jail-based units only as a door opener with counties that are already suing. The edge is speed, outcome data (days to competency, restoration rate) and a staffed, licensed footprint, not a technology moat.
picks.payer_and_signer: Payer: Texas HHSC's private inpatient competency-restoration bed line (about 747 beds a day already contracted), plus equivalent forensic lines in Washington DSHS, Oklahoma ODMHSAS and Colorado CDHS. Signer: HHSC deputy executive commissioner for state hospitals and procurement; the legislature appropriates (next regular session starts January 2027), and the federal court monitors benchmarks.
picks.path_to_100m: 600 beds x $450 x 365 = $98.6M. Example mix by year 6: Texas 350 beds, Washington 150, Oklahoma/Colorado/next-wave state 100. Texas alone is a 1,000+ bed gap I estimate at $160M+ a year; the national unmet need is 3,000-4,000 beds per the pool file (unsourced), so $100M is roughly 15-20% share, at the edge of heroic. Requires 5-year take-or-pay or availability payments to finance leased units. Revenue per full-service bed is about $164k a year; exit multiples are low (Wellpath RS sold at about 0.9x revenue).
picks.competitors_and_edge: Wellpath Recovery Solutions ($425M revenue, 3,000 patients, 70 facilities, creditor-owned), Liberty Healthcare, GEO Group, and likely UHS and Acadia (unverified); HHSC's current private-bed vendors are not named in public sources. Edge: deployable in 6-12 months versus years for state construction ($2.5B for about 680 beds), a price below HHSC's own cost per bed ($412 at Harris's state-hospital comparison, $697 at North Texas State Hospital in 2016), and a clean restoration-outcome record. Edge is thin and copyable by incumbents with buildings.
picks.why_now: Ward v. Muth permanent injunction on 2026-07-07 requires admission within 21 days with four years to comply; HHSC says beds will still fall short; Washington fined about $100M in 2026; Oklahoma began paying $100-$500 a day per waiting person in Oct 2025; Colorado has paid $55M in capped fines through a decree that ends 2027-12-01; Wellpath RS is now creditor-owned, loosening an incumbent.
picks.moat: Thin: licensed and permitted beds, site and lease agreements, 3-5 year contracts, a credentialed staff pool and a restoration-outcome record. A rival with owned buildings can copy it; the defence is speed to first contract and track record.
picks.biggest_open_risk: The Fifth Circuit narrows or reverses Ward v. Muth (the state has asked it to pause benchmarks, argues the Constitution never required the remedy, and an earlier 2012 21-day order was paused), removing the urgency that moves Texas from building to buying.
picks.cheapest_next_test: File a Texas Public Information Act request to HHSC for every private inpatient competency-restoration contract (vendor, per diem, beds, term, occupancy) and the SB 528 cost-comparison report; read the benchmark order and any Fifth Circuit stay ruling on the docket; get three modular or leased-unit quotes and staffing plans for a 60-bed unit; call the Dallas and Bexar sheriffs and HHSC contract management.

result.pool_note: The vendor-bankruptcy shock produced vendor swaps, not new structures, so ideas needing buyers to restructure stalled. Gross pass-through revenue (primes, drugs, fee-only, MGA premium) hid small net revenue. The survivor had a court mandate, an existing budget line and physical capacity. Round-1 pattern repeated: thin moats everywhere.

ideas.title: Werkhof
ideas.one_liner: A net-lease landlord that buys the owner's privately held operating building at the moment the company is sold and leases it back to the successor for 15-20 years, so the owner exits clean and the buyer needs about a third less financing.
ideas.customer: Owner-managers aged 58-68 who hold the Betriebsimmobilie personally or in a Besitz-KG and rent it to their own GmbH, and the successors who cannot fund company plus building.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The successor's operating company pays rent from operating costs (it replaces debt service). Signers: the retiring Inhaber (sale) and the successor Geschaeftsfuehrer (lease); the Steuerberater recommends. Capital side: a Pfandbrief or insurer lender's credit committee plus equity LPs.
ideas.problem: The building is the second-largest asset and the hidden deal-killer. A building a shareholder rents to his GmbH is usually a Betriebsaufspaltung (BFH treats it as an essential operating asset). When the shares go to an unrelated buyer the link ends and hidden reserves in the building can become taxable (CMS Law, Steuerschroeder). The owner is left with three bad choices: sell building with company (successor cannot fund both), cash it out taxed, or stay landlord to a stranger.
ideas.solution: A standardised, notarised sale (of the building, or the Besitz entity where that is tax-better) to Werkhof at closing, with a triple-net 15-20 year indexed lease to the new owner and a tenant buy-back option. The first product is a tax-first term sheet built with the owner's Steuerberater, not a price quote.
ideas.why_now: KfW Jan 2026: prices are up 34% since 2019 to an average EUR 499k, while the 077 loan funds only 35% of costs up to EUR 500k and only for natural persons, so the building is the cheque that breaks the financing stack. 119,000 short-term successions are already agreed or in talks. E&Y found 11.6% of Mittelstaendler could imagine selling real estate.
ideas.wedge: Standardised sale-and-leaseback of buildings worth EUR 0.5-2.5M (Handwerk, light industry, wholesale) tied to an identified successor. First 10 customers via 10-15 Steuerberater kanzleien in Bavaria and NRW (largest absolute handover counts per IfM).
ideas.path_to_100m: Rent of EUR 87M ($100M) at a 7% net initial yield (my assumption for thin-credit single tenants) = EUR 1.24B of buildings. At EUR 1.2M average that is about 1,030 assets, built at 225 a year over 4.6 years. If 25% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year (IfM) have an owner-held building (my assumption; no national statistic found, only that Mittelstand firms own about 75% of used property), that is 9,300 a year, so Werkhof needs about 2.4% of them. Capital: about EUR 370-430M equity plus EUR 800-870M secured debt, so it needs a real-estate sponsor, not a seed round.
ideas.who_does_it_today: DAL Deutsche Anlagen-Leasing (Sparkassen-Finanzgruppe) markets Immobilienleasing for succession; Nord Leasing does machinery sale-and-rent-back; Sparkassen sell Immobilien-Leasing (a leasing executive says they are often called 'as an emergency anchor' late). Free substitute: the owner keeps the building and rents it to the successor, which is the default today. I did not find DAL's minimum ticket.
ideas.why_they_lose: Leasing arms are project-driven and sold at the Berater's discretion, not a standard small-ticket product with a Steuerberater channel. Sparkassen want the building loan and the deposits, not a buyer that removes both. Nobody owns the tax-first workflow.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (cost of capital, standard documents) plus switching costs (15-20 year leases); counter-positioning against bank-owned leasing arms.
ideas.earned_secret: In small-company sales the argument is rarely about price. It is about what happens to the building after tax. A buyer of the building that lets the owner pick the cheapest tax path unlocks deals that otherwise die in the Steuerberater's office.
ideas.first_90_days: Get a written tax memo on the three exit paths from two Steuerberater firms. Sign 10 kanzleien for a free Immobilien-Check. Underwrite 5 live buildings. Get one Pfandbrief-bank term sheet on a pooled facility. Draft the notarial template. Kill risks: lender appetite for small single-tenant assets, tax structure too expensive for most owners, yield above 7% for weak tenants.

ideas.title: Verkaufsreif
ideas.one_liner: A 6-24 month 'make it sellable' programme for owners 58-66 that is paid only at closing (about 9-10% of price), producing audited normalised earnings and the first price database for sub-EUR 2M firms.
ideas.customer: Owner-managed firms with 3-30 employees, 1-3 years before the planned exit.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The seller-owner, from sale proceeds at closing (a transaction cost netted from the price). Signer: the Inhaber, introduced by the Steuerberater. Later buyers (holding vehicles, lenders) pay for data access.
ideas.problem: Deals die 24 months before the negotiation: owners stop investing (KfW: about -32% investment in firms with short-term plans), the owner is the only relationship holder, books are tax-minimised so buyers cannot see earnings, and expectations meet reality only at LOI (owner median 0.6x revenue versus a Bau/Handwerk market range of 0.25-0.50x). KfW itself says there is no generally accepted pricing scheme. The 42% of closure planners who cite bureaucracy never start.
ideas.solution: A fixed programme: normalised-EBITDA package; install a Prokurist or Betriebsleiter and move key customer relationships into the firm; e-invoice/GoBD/ERP clean-up; capture the owner's tacit knowledge; then run a buyer process into a pool of pre-qualified buyers (Meisterwerk and Teamkauf below, PE platforms, strategics, individuals). The platform fronts the cost and is repaid at closing.
ideas.why_now: Closures exceed successions for the first time (KfW Jan 2026); 186,000 firms plan to hand over by end-2026; 11% see modernisation cost as a hurdle; nexxt-change 2.0 will make listings free and commodity, so paid value moves to readiness and certainty.
ideas.wedge: Handwerk and small trade/wholesale firms with EUR 0.8-4M revenue. First 10 from a Steuerberater panel and an HWK Nachfolgemoderator in one region.
ideas.path_to_100m: 9-10% of an average EUR 450,000 price = EUR 40,500-45,000 a closing. EUR 87M needs 1,930-2,150 closings a year = 5.2-5.8% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year (about 2x the roughly 1,100 a year nexxt-change has initiated). Staffing: about 300 transaction managers at 7 closings each. It needs a 45-55% close rate; it is the only fee model in this pool that gets near $100M without heroic share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Unternehmensmakler and M&A boutiques (e.g. Nachfolgekontor), IHK/HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren (free), nexxt-change (free, 431 regional partners), Steuerberater with DATEV Vermoegensnachfolge and wevalue valuation on the DATEV Marktplatz, Sparkassen advisers.
ideas.why_they_lose: Brokers are paid only at closing, so they cannot fund 12-24 months of preparation. Chambers are free and cannot operate. Steuerberater are barred from referral shares (section 9 StBerG, 'sonstige Vorteile') and from most success fees (section 9a, narrow exceptions, from memory), and the sale may cost them the client. DATEV's valuation is a tax valuation, not a market price.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the only dataset of normalised earnings to realised prices below EUR 2M) plus process power.
ideas.earned_secret: The price gap and the owner-dependence are curable, but only if someone is willing to work for free for two years and be repaid out of the closing. Nobody in the chain has that incentive.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 10 owners with 24-month exclusivity and a tail clause (to stop disintermediation). Build the normalisation template with two Steuerberater. Price 20 closed comps from advisers. Recruit 5 buyers. Get counsel on the fee premise. Kill risks: disintermediation after the free work; programme cost per closing above EUR 15k.

ideas.title: Meisterwerk
ideas.one_liner: A steward-owned, permanent-capital buyer of micro Handwerk and technical-service firms (electrical testing, fire protection, heating and water service, lift maintenance), priced below what private equity can touch, with a Meister equity ladder for the people who run them.
ideas.customer: Owners 58-68 of firms with EUR 0.8-2.5M revenue and recurring inspection and service contracts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The customers of the firms (building owners, property managers, small industry) pay from maintenance budgets. Capital comes from permanent-capital LPs (Versorgungswerk or family office CIO). Signer on each deal: the seller-owner.
ideas.problem: A-trades in Germany need a Meister as owner or Betriebsleiter on the Handwerksrolle (from memory, HwO section 7; verify). When the owner retires, the licence leaves with him. PE platforms want EBITDA above EUR 1M and a sale in 4-6 years; micro firms are below that and sellers fear a flip.
ideas.solution: Buy at 0.25-0.50x revenue (FINANCE range) with half deferred against retention of service contracts. The old Meister stays 2-3 years as Betriebsleiter (a Ludwig-Froehler-Institut finding). The firm sponsors a Geselle to Meister, who earns equity in the local firm over 5 years. Central back office, procurement, compliance scheduling and insurance. No AI claim.
ideas.why_now: HWK Dortmund spring 2026: 33% of Handwerk firms plan a handover within 5 years. About 100,000 unfilled Handwerk positions (KOFA 7/2026). KfW: owners value continuity (EBO 28%, MBO 24% considered). BMJV/BMF key points for a GmbH mit gebundenem Vermoegen (Feb-Mar 2026), though no draft bill is confirmed.
ideas.wedge: Elektro and SHK firms with periodic-inspection books in two regions; the first 10 acquisitions from HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren.
ideas.path_to_100m: 60 firms x EUR 1.5M revenue = EUR 90M ($103.5M). Purchase price EUR 22-45M in total (0.25-0.50x revenue) plus working capital; 12 deals a year over 5 years. This needs about 0.03% of handovers, so the limit is Meister supply and integration, not market share. Revenue is bought; expect a 6-9% operating margin. This is the least original idea here and the surest path to $100M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: HWP Handwerkspartner (Adiuva to Goldbeck Robens), Builtech Group, Konzmann Gruppe, TBS Brandschutz (DBAG's Fire Holding), FOGTEC (Deutsche Private Equity), svt (Ergon). Free substitute: the owner closes.
ideas.why_they_lose: Fund economics cannot buy EUR 100-200k EBIT firms or promise to hold forever. Banks cannot hold equity. Steuerberater cannot take a commercial role.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against PE (a hold-forever promise), scale economies in back office and procurement, and a Meister pipeline as a cornered resource.
ideas.earned_secret: In Handwerk the Meister is the asset, not the building or the customer list. Whoever solves Meister succession can buy the rest cheaply.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign term sheets with 3 sellers. Line up EUR 15M of seed permanent capital. Draft the Meister-equity ladder. Check contract recurrence on real customer books (DGUV V3 intervals are risk-based, not fixed). Kill risks: customers drift away on the owner's exit; PE moves down-market.

ideas.title: Netzplan
ideas.one_liner: A group of retiring owner-led planning, survey and permit offices that sells fixed-price 'planned and permitted kilometre of route' to distribution-grid operators and Stadtwerke.
ideas.customer: Distribution-grid operators and municipal utilities with rate-base-funded grid expansion.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The DSO's approved investment budget (capital costs recognised in the revenue cap). Signer: head of grid construction or of procurement; the municipal Tiefbauamt for Sondervermoegen work.
ideas.problem: The bottleneck of the money is planning and supervision, not shovels. IW: about 10,000 planning and supervision experts missing; 81% of planning vacancies unfilled (Oct 2025); Tiefbau needs about 18% more capacity. BDEW: DSO investment rises from EUR 8.6B (2024) to EUR 15.4B a year by 2030. Small owner-led offices that hold local permit knowledge are retiring.
ideas.solution: Buy the offices and keep the owners as employees (Aktivrente is tax-free to employees, not to the self-employed). Install one toolchain (digitised route data, standard permit packs). Sell per-route-kilometre or per-connection-batch fixed prices instead of hours.
ideas.why_now: The BDEW grid-investment path; the EUR 500B Sondervermoegen (about EUR 30B a year of construction orders per IW); Aktivrente from 2026; the planner shortage.
ideas.wedge: Hausanschluss and Trassen planning for 3 mid-size Stadtwerke; the first acquisitions are 2 offices with EUR 2-3M revenue.
ideas.path_to_100m: Planning/survey/permit/supervision at about 10-12% of grid capex (my assumption) = EUR 1.5-1.85B a year by 2030, plus about EUR 1.9B on Sondervermoegen Tiefbau. EUR 87M is 5-6% of the DSO pool alone, or about 2.5% of both. Build: 25-30 offices at EUR 3M revenue each, bought at 0.56-1.03x revenue = EUR 50-80M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Triton's formicon (Jan 2026), XPartners (Axcel, employee-majority; bought Corall Ingenieure in Aug 2026), large engineers (Sweco, Arcadis, Ramboll, from memory) and DSO in-house teams.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generalist engineering roll-ups sell hours across all building types; none is organised around DSO outcome units. DSOs are rate-regulated and want predictable unit costs.
ideas.moat: Process power (standard toolchain, permit templates) and switching costs through framework contracts.
ideas.earned_secret: Permit knowledge sits in the head of a 62-year-old. It is the scarce input, and the DSO will pay for certainty.
ideas.first_90_days: Hold 3 DSO pilot conversations; identify 10 retiring offices through Ingenieurkammer listings; test unit-price quotes on 5 past projects. Kill risks: an Aug 2026 survey says the Sondervermoegen barely arrives at engineering offices; a VKU poll says only 8% think the DSO target is reachable under current rules; PE is already buying.

ideas.title: Teamkauf
ideas.one_liner: A packaged team buyout for 3-8 employees, using the 100% state-guaranteed 077 loan per partner, a vendor note and a regional participation, plus a shared back office that stays with the firm for a fee on revenue.
ideas.customer: Retiring owners who want continuity, and teams that lack equity, collateral and management bandwidth.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The firm pays a service fee out of operating costs; the origination fee is financed inside the purchase. Signers: the seller-owner (mandate) and the lead Geschaeftsfuehrer of the team.
ideas.problem: KfW says EBO (28%) and MBO (24%) are considered by many but get little attention. Hausbanken lend against collateral and personal guarantees; the Steuerberater cannot take equity or a commercial role; chambers cannot charge; PE cannot do the tickets; 077 is per natural person and covers 35% of costs. Nobody assembles the stack, or stays on as the finance function afterwards.
ideas.solution: A standard vehicle (a holding of employee-partners), a template financing stack (077 per partner as a 'taetige Beteiligung', Buergschaftsbank-backed bank loan, MBG participation, vendor note), governance covenants, and a back office (invoicing, dunning, payroll prep, e-invoice compliance, purchasing, insurance, financing) for about 1.2% of revenue. Right of first offer on partner exit.
ideas.why_now: KfW Jan 2026 (closures exceed successions; EBO and MBO rising). 077 live since Nov 2024. BMJV/BMF key points for a GmbH mit gebundenem Vermoegen in Feb-Mar 2026 (no draft bill confirmed).
ideas.wedge: Firms with 6-20 employees and a clear No. 2 and No. 3 in the team. First 10 via HWK Nachfolgemoderatoren and Steuerberater who already see the employee option.
ideas.path_to_100m: Origination 2.5% of a EUR 400k price (EUR 10k) plus 1.2% of EUR 1.8M revenue (EUR 21.6k a year). A portfolio of about 3,900 firms gives EUR 87M of recurring fees: about 650 closings a year for 6 years = 1.7% of the 37,200 actual handovers a year. Honest caution: only 123 applications for 077 were logged at Buergschaftsbank Baden-Wuerttemberg in 2025, and applicants stay personally liable, which is the real reason employees say no.
ideas.who_does_it_today: I found no dedicated German EBO packager in this run. Pieces exist: Hausbank + Buergschaftsbank + MBG + KfW 077, Steuerberater, and steward-ownership investors (Purpose Evergreen Capital, from memory). UK EOT advisers and US ESOP administrators are analogues.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each incumbent holds one piece and a conflict: collateral culture, no equity role, no fee mandate.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (embedded back office, covenants, right of first offer), scale economies in shared services, counter-positioning against Steuerberater.
ideas.earned_secret: Employees do not fail at buying; they fail in the 18 months after, when nobody is the finance function.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 5 sellers with a visible No. 2; write the stack with one Buergschaftsbank and one MBG; draft the legal template; price the service fee against a part-time Buchhalter. Kill risks: personal liability keeps employees out; demand behind 'considered' is thin.

ideas.title: Aufloesungsboerse
ideas.one_liner: An orderly-closure service that sells the bundle a closing firm leaves behind (its staff, customers, equipment and premises) to neighbours who are short of all four.
ideas.customer: Owners of the roughly 114,000 firms a year that plan to close with no successor; on the other side, growing firms with open positions.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The owner pays a wind-down fee; hiring firms pay placement fees from their personnel budget; buyers pay for customer books and equipment. Signers: the closing owner and the Inhaber of the hiring firm.
ideas.problem: No incumbent earns anything on a firm worth under EUR 100k. M&A boutiques have minimum fees, Steuerberater bill hours, chambers are free and cannot operate, Sparkassen see no credit, and nexxt-change matches going concerns. Yet Handwerk has about 200,000 open positions (ZDH) and roughly 100,000 unfillable ones (KOFA 7/2026).
ideas.solution: A fixed wind-down package (Schlussbilanz and archive with a partner Steuerberater, Gewerbeabmeldung, notices, GoBD archive, run-off cover) that the owner can fund from selling the bundle. Selective hiring of staff by neighbours (not an entity transfer, to stay outside section 613a BGB), customer-by-customer consent for the customer book, and an equipment and vehicle auction channel.
ideas.why_now: 2026 is the first year planned closures exceed planned successions; KfW says 47% of closure planners cite no family interest and 42% cite bureaucracy.
ideas.wedge: Handwerk closures in regions with the most open positions. First 10 via HWK Betriebsberater and Steuerberater who tell clients 'it is not worth anything'.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per client: EUR 2.5k wind-down fee (all clients) plus, for the 45% with a bundle, about EUR 13.5k (1.8 hires x EUR 5k, EUR 3k customer-book commission, EUR 1.5k equipment) = about EUR 8.6k average. EUR 87M needs about 10,100 clients a year = about 9% of the 114,000 planned closures (about 12% of the 80,000 that actually close, my assumption). That is close to heroic: it works only with strong software and as the feeder for Meisterwerk and Teamkauf.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody as a bundle. Pieces: nexxt-change, HWK Betriebsboersen (from memory), Surplex/Troostwijk machinery auctions (from memory), Kleinanzeigen, the Arbeitsagentur, Steuerberater for the wind-down.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each earns nothing on its piece and none can sell the whole.
ideas.moat: Network economies (closing supply meets hiring demand in the same region) plus regional vacancy data.
ideas.earned_secret: A closing firm's value is not on its balance sheet. It is its Gesellen and its customer list, and the buyers are the neighbours who cannot hire.
ideas.first_90_days: Run 20 closures end to end in one region; get a labour-law opinion on selective hiring versus section 613a; sign 15 hiring firms. Kill risks: the 613a reading; customers don't follow; most closers are solo operators with no staff (I found no headcount data for closers).

ideas.title: Zulieferwerk
ideas.one_liner: An acquirer-modernizer of owner-led precision-machining shops that qualifies them as second-source suppliers for defence primes.
ideas.customer: Primes and tier-1s that need machined parts (Rheinmetall says it has about 23,000 suppliers).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Strategic procurement at the prime, through multi-year framework supply contracts. Signer: head of purchasing or supply chain. On acquisition: the seller-owner.
ideas.problem: The constraint is qualification, not orders (quality systems such as AS/EN 9100, security clearance, traceability, first-article approval, export controls). A 58-year-old Zerspanungsunternehmer with idle 5-axis capacity cannot afford 18-36 months of qualification and has no successor.
ideas.solution: Buy the shop at 0.38-0.69x revenue, fund the qualification, bring the prime's framework contract before closing where possible, and keep the owner on.
ideas.why_now: German rearmament, the auto-supplier job losses, VW Osnabrueck in talks with defence firms, Rheinmetall selling its auto division to Aequita for EUR 350M to focus on defence, and IHK Stuttgart procurement seminars up from a few to 300-400 attendees.
ideas.wedge: Turned-part and 5-axis shops with EUR 4-8M revenue and an existing prime as customer.
ideas.path_to_100m: 15 shops x EUR 6M = EUR 90M. Cost EUR 35-50M to buy plus EUR 10-15M qualification. Execution-limited, not share-limited.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mutares (turnarounds, defence units such as Magirus), Pinova Capital (industrial tech, EUR 10-75M revenue), Aurelius, Rheinmetall itself.
ideas.why_they_lose: Mutares and Aurelius buy distress, not healthy owner-led shops. Primes cannot buy suppliers without a conflict. Banks hesitate on defence exposure (from memory).
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (qualified capacity) and switching costs once qualified.
ideas.earned_secret: Spare capacity is worthless until it is certified. Certification is what the buyer adds.
ideas.first_90_days: Sit with 3 primes' purchasing teams; get a qualification-cost estimate from a lead auditor; find 5 shops. Kill risk: sources do not show Mittelstand gains yet (produktion.de: value distribution not clear before 2027; Stuttgarter Zeitung: auto jobs are not absorbed). This fails the digest's gate unless a prime commits.

ideas.title: Anschluss
ideas.one_liner: Buy the sites of closing Mittelstand plants whose value to the owner is a building but to a battery, charging or data-centre developer is an existing grid connection.
ideas.customer: Closing manufacturers, bakeries, cold stores and workshops with a medium-voltage connection; on the other side, storage, truck-charging, light-industry and defence tenants.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Tenants and developers from their site budgets. Signer: their head of grid or real estate.
ideas.problem: E.ON reports more than 10,000 large-battery connection requests (about 500 GW) and more than 500 data-centre projects (about 70 GW). Oldenburg IHK reports delays of years. The cabinet adopted the Netzpaket on 29 Jul 2026 (priority and reservation rules). An existing connection is the scarce input, and the closing owner prices only a building.
ideas.solution: Buy or option the site at a price above building value, secure the Anschlussnutzung, and re-let or develop.
ideas.why_now: The Netzpaket, the connection queue, and 114,000 planned closures a year.
ideas.wedge: Sites with 0.4-2 MVA connections in grid-constrained regions. First 10 via HWK, IHK and local Steuerberater.
ideas.path_to_100m: 150 sites a year at EUR 1.2M = EUR 180M a year; after 6 years about EUR 1.08B at 8% yield on cost = EUR 87M. Assumption: 3-5% of the 114,000 closers have a connection of 400 kVA or more, so 150 a year is 3-4% of that group.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Developers buy land directly; DSOs; real-estate developers. I found no one systematically buying closing SMEs for connection rights (a negative result, not proof of a gap).
ideas.why_they_lose: Developers look at greenfield; closers don't know what they have; DSOs cannot trade capacity.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (connection rights) and speed.
ideas.earned_secret: The queue is long, and a closing neighbour has already waited in it.
ideas.first_90_days: Get a written opinion from a grid lawyer on whether capacity survives owner change and change of use under the Netzpaket; survey 50 closures for connection size; sign a battery developer for 3 sites. Kill risk: if capacity lapses on closure or change of use, the idea is dead. It overlaps with Werkhof as a real-estate model.

ideas.title: Signed-Off: the QA-accountable AI engineering house
ideas.one_liner: Sell nuclear plants finished, signed, Appendix B-compliant engineering deliverables at a fixed price per deliverable, produced by an AI pipeline that sits inside a qualified quality program, instead of selling another AI tool or more hourly engineers.
ideas.customer: Design and fleet engineering organizations at the ~25 owner-operators. Start with single-site and restart operators with thin benches (EUCG counts 10 'one plant' operators; e.g. Energy Northwest, Evergy/Wolf Creek, Ameren/Callaway, Holtec/Palisades, Constellation/Crane, NextEra/Duane Arnold; names from background knowledge).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contracted engineering and supplemental-staff lines in O&M plus project engineering inside the $7.59B 2025 capital budget (NEI/EUCG, Aug 2026). Signer: Director of Design Engineering or VP Engineering. Supply Chain adds the firm to the Approved Supplier List and the QA director must accept the quality program.
ideas.problem: Capital spend jumped 24% in 2025 and ~30 uprates, three restarts and 20+ license renewals queue behind a shrinking engineer pool. The work product (50.59 screenings and evaluations, calculation revisions, engineering change packages, license-amendment sections) must be traceable, independently verified and issued by an organization under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B. AI tools exist (Nuclearn lists an 'Engineering AI' product) but a tool's output cannot be used on safety-related work until a qualified organization owns it, so engineers redo it by hand and overflow goes out hourly to Sargent & Lundy-class firms.
ideas.solution: An engineering supplier with (a) its own NQA-1/Appendix B program, listed on customers' Approved Supplier Lists after a NUPIC-style joint audit; (b) a version-locked AI drafting and checking stack verified under NQA-1 software QA; (c) nuclear-qualified engineers who review and sign every output; (d) a fixed price per deliverable with a rework guarantee. Over time the verified calculation and evaluation templates per plant design become a reusable library, then new-build and licensing work.
ideas.why_now: Capital +24% in 2025 and uprate capex up from $66M (2022) to $365M (2025) meet a thin engineer bench. A DOE/INL/ANL/Microsoft/Everstar test turned a 4-6 week license-application drafting task into one day (208-page draft). Hyperscaler-priced power lets owners afford capital but not engineers.
ideas.wedge: 50.59 screenings and calculation revisions (high volume, bounded) for 2-3 single-site operators, with the plant's own engineer signing the first pilots (quality-related scope) while the QA program and ASL listing are built. Faster route: buy or white-label a 30-100 person ASL-listed engineering boutique and run under its QA program. First 10 customers: single-plant operators plus the three restarts.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION (no published figure found): outsourced nuclear engineering is ~10% of capital ($0.76B) plus ~5% of non-labor operating ($0.37B), about $1.1B/yr; add the uprate/restart wave (2.3 GW x ~$4.8k/kW is ~$11B, 8-10% engineering is ~$1B over 5 years, ~$200M/yr). Pool ~$1.3-1.4B/yr by 2028-30. $100M is ~7% of it (~400 billable-engineer equivalents at ~$250k); because deliverables are priced at a discount to hourly, volume share is ~10-12%. Upside: ~25 funded reactor developers spend tens of millions each on engineering and licensing. A software-only subscription across ~70 facilities (Nuclearn-style) caps at ~$35-70M (my arithmetic at $0.5-1M per site), which is why the service model is the path.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hourly engineering firms: Sargent & Lundy (ENR #1 in nuclear plants, eight times in a decade), Enercon (self-described top 3), Jensen Hughes (ENR #4), Framatome, Westinghouse, Bechtel, Aptim; owner in-house design engineering. AI tools: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, 'over 70 facilities', annual per-product subscription), Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, Diablo Canyon), Everstar ($4M pre-seed, Gordian, DOE drafting test). No one found selling QA-accountable deliverables.
ideas.why_they_lose: Hourly firms cannot cut hours without cutting revenue. Tool vendors do not carry QA accountability or an engineer's signature. Frontier labs will not hold an Appendix B program. Owners will not accept unowned output on safety-related work.
ideas.moat: Switching costs plus process power: ASL status takes 12-24 months of audits, each owner's QA acceptance and per-plant verified templates lock in; counter-positioning against hourly billers. Reached by passing the first supplier audits and accumulating a signed-deliverable history.
ideas.earned_secret: Nobody in nuclear buys AI; they buy a name on the signature block. The binding constraint is who is accountable under Appendix B, not model quality, which is why every AI product stays stuck on search and screening. The business is the QA program. (Hypothesis from the insider persona; validate in first 15 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 15 design-engineering directors and QA managers and 2 ASL-listed boutiques (acquire or white-label). Write the NQA-1 software-QA plan. Run a paid pilot of ~20 50.59 screenings with 1-2 single-site operators, plant engineer signing; measure hours saved and rework. Schedule the supplier audit. Legal gate: Appendix B Criterion VII makes the licensee responsible for suppliers; state PE rules apply; no NRC rule found barring QA-controlled AI-assisted analysis (confirm with counsel).

ideas.title: Dose Ledger: the nuclear traveler network
ideas.one_liner: A W-2 employer-of-record network of radiation-protection technicians, welders, pipefitters, NDE and I&C techs that chains workers across every outage in the country, with a portable credential and dose-headroom ledger, so plants get badged crews in days and workers get ~40 weeks of work a year.
ideas.customer: Outage managers and site-support directors at ~55 nuclear sites, plus the integrated outage primes (Westinghouse, Framatome, GE Vernova Hitachi) that subcontract labor; later restarts and new-build owners.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Supplemental-labor lines in outage O&M. Signer: Outage Manager or Director of Site Support; Supply Chain executes the MSA; merchant CFOs care because outage days are worth ~$1.6-2.4M each.
ideas.problem: A refueling outage brings 1,000-1,400 temporary workers (Entergy ANO 1,300; Columbia Generating Station 1,400 for a 40-day outage; Davis-Besse 1,000+). Outage seasons cluster, so every plant bids for the same people at once; the senior contract RP technician pool shrank ~37% in three years (Health Physics, 2022); travelers idle between seasons and quit; each site re-badges a worker (background, fitness-for-duty, training, dose history), which sits on the outage critical path.
ideas.solution: Employer-of-record payroll; a credential vault (certifications, training, access status, respirator fit); a dose-headroom ledger showing remaining annual dose so planners see who can take a high-dose job; a scheduler that chains workers across plants' outage calendars; pre-clearance workflows so site badging takes days. Expand to training pipelines (Navy nukes, veterans), housing/per diem, and a senior-expert bench for restarts and new builds.
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler-priced power raises an outage day to ~$1.6-2.4M for a 1.1 GW unit at $60-90/MWh (arithmetic), so labor readiness is the cheapest lever. Palisades, Crane and Duane Arnold restarts and new builds compete for the same people. NRC's July 2026 ALARA proposal keeps dose limits unchanged but may reduce RP hours (risk).
ideas.wedge: Senior RP technicians, the scarcest trade, for spring 2027 outages (March-May) at 2-3 single-site operators or one integrated prime. First 10 customers: single-site operators plus one OEM outage organization.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~50 outages/yr (inference from 94 reactors on 18-24 month cycles) x 1,000-1,400 temporary workers = ~50-70k worker-outages. At ~300-350 hours x ~$75/hr blended bill rate (Vogtle outage posting: senior RPT $39.52-44.72/hr), ~$22-26k per worker-outage, so outage temp labor is ~$1.2-1.6B/yr (cross-check: older trade figures put direct outage cost at $300-800k/day x ~38 days = $11-30M per outage). $100M of billings is ~4,000-4,500 worker-outages, ~7% share. Gross margin only ~15-20%, so this is a $100M-revenue business, not a $100M-profit one, unless the ledger, training, payroll and housing layers earn more.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Integrated outage primes: Westinghouse (10-year integrated outage contract with Xcel), Framatome (integrated outage services for FENOC), GE Vernova Hitachi (>$70M Browns Ferry outage services); Westinghouse direct-hire outage technician postings; NukeWorker job board; a long tail of regional craft and RP staffing firms (not individually verified). No funded startup found doing nuclear credentialing or outage staffing.
ideas.why_they_lose: Staffing firms are paid per head per outage and see only their own customers' schedules. Merchant rivals do not share outage calendars, so nobody can chain a worker into 40 weeks. Badging is rebuilt site by site.
ideas.moat: Network economies (two-sided: workers and plants) plus cornered resource (the best few thousand travelers' loyalty and their dose/credential histories). Commodity staffing is the failure mode.
ideas.earned_secret: The shortage is a synchronization and paperwork problem as much as a headcount problem: outage windows cluster so travelers idle and quit, and a worker's remaining annual dose headroom and badge status, not skills, decide who can take a job. Whoever sees every schedule sells continuity and speed. (Hypothesis; validate in first 20 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 outage managers/RP supervisors and 30 travelers. Build the credential and dose-ledger MVP with ~100 RP techs. Sign an LOI with one single-site operator or integrated prime for spring 2027. Register as employer of record (W-2, workers' comp, staffing licensing). Legal gate: 10 CFR 73.56 access authorization and Part 26 fitness-for-duty stay licensee-run programs; Part 20 dose-record rules; worker classification must be W-2.

ideas.title: Certified Cell: Hadrian for nuclear (the automated NQA-1 parts factory)
ideas.one_liner: Transfer the defense neo-prime playbook (Hadrian-style automated precision-machining factories selling into supply-constrained primes) into nuclear: a factory whose machine-control and inspection systems write the Appendix B/NQA-1 paper trail as they cut, so certified capacity becomes the product.
ideas.customer: Westinghouse and its AP1000 supply base, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Flowserve-class valve/pump OEMs, reactor developers (TerraPower, X-energy, Kairos), and fleet owners' supply chains (replacement internals, fasteners, supports, instrument fittings).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Supply Chain Officer or VP Procurement at the OEM/developer, from component procurement in capital budgets. Fleet side: Director of Supply Chain with engineering acceptance.
ideas.problem: Few shops hold ASME N-type certificates or NQA-1 programs, so a new-build and uprate wave hits a thin sub-tier. DOE conditional loans of $17.5B (June 2026; up to five loans of two reactors each) pull long-lead buying forward by up to three years. Valar and Radiant are hiring supplier-quality engineers because the qualified base is small. April 2026 Section 232 changes (25% on full value for most metal derivatives, 50% for near-all-metal) push buyers toward domestic content.
ideas.solution: A high-mix, low-volume automated machining and inspection factory: material heat traceability, in-process inspection and certificates generated by the system; ASME certification and an NQA-1 certificate; pre-dedicated stock of fleet long-tail parts; anchor customer offtake before building.
ideas.why_now: First sustained nuclear order book in ~40 years, federal loans financing long-lead buys, tariffs, and defense-tech investors who proved the automated-factory model but have not looked at nuclear.
ideas.wedge: Fasteners, valve and pump internals, supports and instrument fittings for AP1000 and developer orders, qualified through one anchor customer; fleet long tail follows. First 10 customers: Westinghouse tier-1s, BWXT, 3-4 reactor developers, and OEMs short of capacity.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: 8-12% of the $17.5B long-lead value is machined/fabricated sub-tier content outside the big forgings: ~$1.4-2.1B over ~6 years, $230-350M/yr. Add the fleet long tail: parts are ~25% of ($7.59B capital + ~$7.5B non-labor operating), ~$3.8B, of which 20-25% is OEM-unsupported (Rolls-Royce study), ~$0.8-0.9B. $100M is one large factory (~150-200 cells) and ~15-20% of the combined flow; capital need ~$50-100M. Honest verdict: big only with an anchor offtake from Westinghouse, BWXT or a developer.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Dedicators/distributors that do not make parts: Park Nuclear (Oak Ridge dedication facility), ATC Nuclear, Nuclear Logistics. OEM aftermarket: Curtiss-Wright (commercial nuclear a stated growth driver; ~$300M base unverified), Flowserve, Velan, Crane. Family-owned qualified machine shops. Kairos built its own U-stamp vessel shop. Hadrian is defense/aerospace only.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs prioritize new-build and cannot add capacity fast. Family shops cannot fund automation plus QA overhead. Dedicators and distributors do not manufacture.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (certified, audited capacity that takes 18-24 months to replicate) plus process power (automated records) plus scale economies; reached via ASME/NQA-1 certification and an anchor offtake.
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce thing is not machine time but certified, auditable lots: the paperwork twin of a safety-related part costs more than the metal, so a factory that generates the paperwork automatically turns a compliance tax into a moat. Caution: 10 CFR 50.69 can move up to 75% of safety-related components (EPRI pilot result) out of special treatment, so target Class 1/2, pressure-boundary and new-build content, not the whole fleet tail.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick the 50 part families with the most backorders from two Westinghouse-qualified suppliers and one developer. Secure an anchor LOI. Identify a state with an existing ASME-certified shop to partner with or acquire. Draft the NQA-1 program. Apply for state/DOE incentives. Legal gate: ASME Section III/NCA-3800 certification, Part 21 reporting, customer ASL audits, Buy-American/domestic-content rules.

ideas.title: One Audit: a supplier-paid shared accreditation for nuclear (Nadcap for nuclear)
ideas.one_liner: Aerospace solved duplicate supplier audits in 1990 with Nadcap (suppliers pay once, every prime accepts). Do the same for the nuclear supply chain across competing primes and ~25 funded developers.
ideas.customer: Subscribers: Westinghouse, Bechtel, Fluor, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, TVA, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos. Accreditation payers: the suppliers themselves (machine shops, foundries, welders, test labs).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Supplier President/QA Manager pays fees; subscribers' Chief Supply Chain Officers pay annual subscriptions from supplier-quality budgets.
ideas.problem: Every developer builds its own supplier-quality team (Valar and Radiant job posts list supplier qualification, audits and dedication protocols) and re-audits the same shops. NUPIC (utility-run joint audits, formed 1989, relied on by the NRC) covers utilities, not competing OEMs, EPCs and developers.
ideas.solution: A neutral registry plus audit program: one standard checklist mapped to NQA-1, ASME NCA-3800 and ISO 19443; accredited auditors; a shared eAuditNet-style database; a 'QA program in a box' for aerospace and oil-and-gas shops converting to nuclear; optional dedication testing labs.
ideas.why_now: DOE-financed AP1000 long-lead buying and ~25 funded developers racing DOE and NRC clocks all need qualified suppliers at once.
ideas.wedge: Sell the 'QA program in a box' and shared assessments to 3-5 founding subscribers (one OEM, one EPC, two developers) who pay for the first 25 supplier assessments; convert to accreditation when a utility QA organization accepts it as survey input.
ideas.path_to_100m: Nadcap precedent: >1,350 accredited suppliers by 2007, >6,900 active accreditations and 53 subscribing OEMs by 2015-16, ~40% fewer audits (PRI-commissioned survey). ASSUMPTION (no published count found): 2,500-3,500 US and allied nuclear-qualified or aspiring suppliers x $20-30k/yr = $50-105M, plus ~60 primes/developers x $250k = $15M, plus QA-in-a-box services. Stretch: needs near-universal adoption and non-US scope (Canada, UK, Poland).
ideas.who_does_it_today: NUPIC (utility joint audits), ASME N-stamp and NQA-1 certificate programs, DOE's own consolidated audit program, third-party inspection firms (not individually verified), and each developer's in-house supplier-quality team.
ideas.why_they_lose: NUPIC's members are utilities that cannot extend audit liability to competing vendors; competing primes will not share audit findings with each other; ASME certifies capability but not ongoing process performance. No incumbent has a neutral position.
ideas.moat: Network economies and switching costs once primes require the accreditation; counter-positioning against each prime's in-house audit team. Reached by signing founding subscribers who commit to accept it.
ideas.earned_secret: The fix is not technology but a neutral party two competing primes both trust, with the supplier paying once. Boeing and Airbus both subscribed to Nadcap for exactly that reason.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 founding subscribers. Recruit 6 ex-NUPIC lead auditors. Run 10 pilot assessments. Ask 1 utility QA organization to confirm acceptability as survey input. Legal gate: antitrust review of shared-audit information exchange (Nadcap/PRI precedent) and licensee acceptance under Appendix B Criterion VII.

ideas.title: Day Rate: the performance-priced outage prime
ideas.one_liner: A challenger outage prime that earns a base fee plus a bonus or penalty per outage day against a P50 baseline, backed by its own critical-path dataset; incumbent primes cannot copy it because they earn on emergent work.
ideas.customer: Site VPs and fleet outage directors, starting with single-site and mid-size operators whose integrated outage contracts come up for renewal.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Outage O&M and capital budgets. Signer: Chief Nuclear Officer or Site VP; for merchant owners the CFO cares because a day of a 1.1 GW unit is ~$1.6-2.4M (arithmetic at $60-90/MWh).
ideas.problem: Outage contracts are typically fixed-price for baseline scope and time-and-materials for the rest (BWXT 10-K language), so emergent work is the incumbents' profit center. Average outage length was ~38 days in an older NEI figure while individual operators showed 19-26 day outages in 2008-2011 SEC filings. Trade figures put direct cost at $300-800k/day plus ~$1M/day replacement power; hyperscaler pricing pushes that higher.
ideas.solution: A fixed-fee-plus-days-saved integrated outage contract, outage control software (critical path, work-package readiness, mobilization, laydown), a dataset of schedule actuals, downside beyond a cap reinsured or capitalized. Pairs with the traveler network (idea 2).
ideas.why_now: Hyperscaler-priced power roughly doubled the value of a day while incumbents' contracts are long-term and fixed, so owners have a reason to look at renewals.
ideas.wedge: Offer a 'critical-path logistics' sub-scope (containment access, laydown, mobilization) with gain-share on days saved for spring 2027, then expand to full prime at renewal.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~50 outages/yr x ~$25-30M each = $1.3-1.5B/yr of outage spend; four outages a year as prime is $100-120M of mostly pass-through revenue at a 10-15% fee (~8% of outages). The prize: fleet outage-days ~1,750/yr (50 x 35); pulling the slow half from 40 to 28 days saves ~300 days x $1.6-2.4M = $480-720M/yr; a 20% performance fee is $95-145M. The two stack.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Westinghouse (10-year integrated outage services contract with Xcel), Framatome (integrated outage services for FENOC), GE Vernova Hitachi (>$70M Browns Ferry outage services), BWXT-type fixed-scope contractors, Day & Zimmermann (background knowledge, not verified), plus owners' own fleet outage organizations (e.g. Constellation).
ideas.why_they_lose: T&M emergent work is margin; fixed-price scope is already priced against risk; the OEMs are not balance-sheet risk takers on schedule and none will pay penalties for days.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning plus cornered resource (a critical-path dataset incumbents will not build) plus scale; reached by winning the first one or two guaranteed outages.
ideas.earned_secret: Outage length is mostly decided before the outage starts (work-package readiness at T-12 weeks, labor mobilization, tooling, crane and laydown constraints), not during execution. (Hypothesis from the insider persona; I found no source for it, validate in the first 10 interviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Build a duration model from NRC's daily Power Reactor Status reports (public, 30 years). Interview 10 outage managers. Pitch a critical-path-logistics gain-share pilot to 3 operators for spring 2027. Legal gate: liquidated damages in a services contract are not insurance; avoid cash-for-lost-generation structures that could be classified as insurance (round 1's NY DFS lesson).

ideas.title: Second Source: HEICO for nuclear plants
ideas.one_liner: An OEM-neutral second source for the long tail of obsolete safety-related parts, with the reverse-engineering, test and dedication package built once and sold to every plant; OEMs cannot do it because sole-source aftermarket is where their margin is.
ideas.customer: Procurement engineering and supply chain at ~55 sites.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Materials and parts lines in O&M and capital. Signer: Director of Supply Chain with Site Engineering acceptance.
ideas.problem: A Rolls-Royce study estimates 20-25% of nuclear plant components are no longer supported by the original equipment provider, and a plant relies on >100,000 parts. The same commercial item is dedicated separately by each plant that buys it. OEMs have no reason to fix that.
ideas.solution: Reverse-engineer and test equivalents for obsolete I&C cards, relays, transmitters, valve and pump internals; build one dedication package per part, accepted across the fleet through engineering equivalency; hold pre-dedicated stock; sell at 30-40% below OEM; keep the library of qualified alternates as the data asset.
ideas.why_now: License extensions toward 80 years plus uprates increase parts demand, and AI-assisted reverse engineering and additive manufacturing cut engineering cost per part.
ideas.wedge: The 200 most common obsolete part numbers across the top 8 plant designs, starting from two operators' obsolescence lists. First 10 customers: operators with active obsolescence programs.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: parts are ~25% of $15.1B (capital + non-labor operating), ~$3.8B/yr; OEM-unsupported 20-25% is $0.75-0.95B. A second source priced at ~65% of OEM needs $154M of OEM-equivalent volume for $100M of revenue, ~16-20% of the exposed pool. Stretch. Existing proof that $100M+ is possible in this space: Curtiss-Wright's commercial nuclear unit (reported ~$300M, unverified).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Park Nuclear (dedication, seismic and material testing, reverse engineering, new Oak Ridge facility), ATC Nuclear, Nuclear Logistics, Curtiss-Wright, Westinghouse and Framatome dedication services, Nuclearn 'Parts AI', Nuclear Utility Obsolescence Group, USA Inc. co-op, PIM pool and the rapidpartsmart network.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs will not release drawings or price at cost; co-ops are non-profit and carry no inventory or liability; mid-size dedicators are sub-scale on engineering.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against OEM aftermarket plus cornered resource (qualified-alternates library with accepted dedication packages); reached by the first ~200 accepted part numbers.
ideas.earned_secret: The dedication package, not the part, is the product. Caution: 10 CFR 50.69 can move up to 75% of safety-related components (EPRI pilot) out of special treatment, shrinking the nuclear-grade premium where adopted; the surviving premium is Class 1/2 and pressure boundary.
ideas.first_90_days: Get 20 obsolete part numbers from two plants, produce dedication packages, have 3 CGD engineers confirm acceptability, take counsel on OEM drawing/patent/trade-secret exposure. Legal gate: Appendix B, Part 21, engineering equivalency; reverse engineering faces IP and contract limits. The aviation PMA analog (HEICO) is background knowledge, not verified here.

ideas.title: Uprate Kit: the fixed-price uprate integrator
ideas.one_liner: Become integrator-of-record for hyperscaler-funded uprates: productize standard uprate kits per plant type and sell megawatts delivered at a fixed price and date.
ideas.customer: Owners with uprate pipelines in NRC's expected-applications table: Constellation, Duke (Brunswick, McGuire, Catawba), PSEG (Salem), Southern (Hatch), Vistra.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Uprate capital project budgets (hyperscaler-backed). Signer: VP Nuclear Engineering/Projects and the CFO; DOE LPO is the lender where loans exist.
ideas.problem: Uprate capex went from $66M (2022) to $365M (2025) and is heading to billions. NRC expects 30 uprates / ~2.3-2.4 GW by 2030-32 against 3-8 GW of potential. Constellation's $4.3B for 890 MW is ~$4.8k/kW versus Browns Ferry's $475M for 14% over 3 units (2018-19) at roughly $1,000/kW. Not like-for-like, but the spread suggests sole-source pricing, scope creep or both. Main turbines, generators, pumps and transformers carry long lead times.
ideas.solution: Feasibility screen for each of 94 reactors, standard retrofit kits by plant type, LAR plan, competitive procurement of long-lead items, reserved equipment slots, and a fixed price per MW delivered with schedule guarantees; optional revenue share on incremental MWh.
ideas.why_now: First large uprate money since 2012 (Google-Constellation 890 MW across 11 units, Meta-Vistra, Amazon-Constellation Calvert Cliffs). The first projects will set the template.
ideas.wedge: A paid feasibility and cost-review package for 3-5 owners built on public data (172 prior uprates), which converts into engineering and procurement for the cheapest 2-3 units.
ideas.path_to_100m: 2.4 GW x $4.8k/kW is ~$11.5B through 2032, about $1.6B/yr; at 8 GW it is ~$38B, $4-5B/yr. As engineering and licensing only (~11%) the base case is ~$180M/yr, so $100M needs ~55% share: not viable. As fixed-price integrator-of-record (revenue gross of equipment) $100M is 2-6% of capex flow: the only version that works. Capital need and warranty risk are high, and owners must give up OEM sole-source relationships. Stretch.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM uprate packages (Westinghouse, GE Vernova Hitachi, Framatome), turbine OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi), engineers (Sargent & Lundy, Bechtel, Burns & McDonnell), owner in-house programs (Constellation). No funded startup found.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs bundle uprates with fuel and services at sole-source prices and will not standardize across competitors' designs. Engineers bill hourly. Owners' in-house teams are the bottleneck.
ideas.moat: Process power (repeatable kits) plus scale economies (reserved equipment slots) plus switching costs (licensing basis); reached by delivering the first two uprates on time.
ideas.earned_secret: Uprate cost sits in a handful of long-lead secondary-side retrofits and licensing analyses, not reactor physics. (Unverified; test with the first three cost reviews.)
ideas.first_90_days: Build the public-data headroom screen. Contact the 5 owners on NRC's expected-uprate list. Sell 1-2 paid feasibility and cost reviews. Legal gate: NRC LAR process, OEM IP licenses, DOE domestic-content guidance (INL, March 2026).

ideas.title: Clock Keeper: pay-on-approval licensing for the 12- and 18-month NRC clocks
ideas.one_liner: Executive Order 14300's clocks (18 months for new reactors, 12 for renewals, enforced through fee-recovery limits) move the bottleneck to the applicant; sell a fixed-price, pay-on-approval licensing submission and RAI-response service with a schedule guarantee.
ideas.customer: Reactor developers (~25 funded), restarts, and fleet owners filing uprate and license-renewal amendments.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Regulatory affairs and licensing budgets plus project capital. Signer: VP Licensing or Chief Regulatory Officer.
ideas.problem: With reviews capped, the NRC's defense against a missed clock is early requests for additional information (RAIs) and strict docketing. The applicant's critical path becomes completeness at docketing and RAI turnaround. Preparing applications takes tens of millions and months.
ideas.solution: A licensing factory: structured regulatory building blocks, a library of RAIs and accepted responses by topic from the NRC's public ADAMS record, former NRC reviewers for mock docketing, and a RAI-response SWAT team. Priced per submission and paid on approval within the clock.
ideas.why_now: EO 14300 (May 2025), NRC reorganization due by end of September 2026, a cluster of final rules September-November 2026, TVA Clinch River approved in 14 months (2026-09-29), rising application volume, and the DOE/INL/ANL/Microsoft/Everstar drafting test.
ideas.wedge: Free mock docketing reviews for 3 applicants due in 2027, converting one to pay-on-approval. First 10 customers: developers and restarts with 2027 filings.
ideas.path_to_100m: ASSUMPTION: ~10 new-reactor applications per year x $30M outsourced preparation = ~$300M/yr; fleet licensing actions ~6 uprate LARs/yr x $20M, ~5 renewals/yr x $25M, plus ~80 smaller actions/yr x $1.5M = ~$365M/yr. Total ~$0.65B/yr; $100M is ~15% of it. Stretch, concentrated in ~35 applicants per year. NRC's own estimate of industry savings from licensing reform is only $15-22M/yr, so the market is applicant preparation spend, not NRC savings.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Licensing consultants (Enercon, Sargent & Lundy, Jensen Hughes, ERIN, Framatome, Westinghouse), law firms (Morgan Lewis), in-house licensing. AI tools: Everstar (Gordian, $4M pre-seed, DOE test), Nuclearn, Atomic Canyon.
ideas.why_they_lose: Consultants and law firms bill hourly and will not take approval risk. Tool vendors sell software, not accountability. Reference-design owners (Westinghouse, GE Vernova Hitachi, TerraPower) keep their own adaptation kits.
ideas.moat: Process power only; all RAIs are public so there is no data moat. Weak. Best treated as an extension of idea 1.
ideas.earned_secret: The NRC clock is enforced through fee-recovery caps, so speed is set by completeness at docketing and the days an applicant takes to answer RAIs, and most RAIs repeat recurring topics (to be validated against ADAMS). It is a process-and-accountability business, not a data business.
ideas.first_90_days: Ingest the ADAMS corpus of RAIs and responses for uprates, renewals and construction permits. Build a topic-level RAI predictor. Offer 3 free mock docketing reviews and convert one to pay-on-approval. Legal gate: 10 CFR 50.9 completeness and accuracy, fee-sharing limits if lawyers are involved, and the practice-of-law boundary.

competitors_found.name: SteadyIQ
competitors_found.what_they_do: Missouri DSS Income Passport for gig and self-employment income, optional for applicants; 18-minute average report

competitors_found.name: Equifax Workforce Solutions (Work Number, TotalVerify)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Incumbent income verification used by about half of states; per-query price hikes of 69-126% in four states
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Government revenue growing but fell about 4% in Q2 2026; about $300M ACV signed mostly with states

competitors_found.name: Deloitte NextGen360 Verification Hub
competitors_found.what_they_do: Multi-source verification hub bundled with state eligibility work
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Free first year under CMS pledge per the idea

verdicts.substitutes: NDNH (SNAP agencies must query it at certification), state UI wage files, the federal Data Services Hub (student and veteran checks now carry Emmy functions), integrators' own source orchestration.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: The $800M Equifax government figure is not in any filing I could open (Q4 2025 8-K gives growth rates only). A savings-share router taking about 30% of savings on a book that includes SSA and non-state revenue yields roughly $30-60M even if half of an assumed $500-800M book moves at a 40-50% discount. The 19% share arithmetic is unverified.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: Antitrust discovery forces payroll providers to open data (plausible, but the case is brought by mortgage lenders and is slow); states mandate a waterfall (moderate); Argyle, Truv and SteadyIQ choose to sell through a router instead of directly to states (low, they already hold state contracts).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Antitrust case is real (E.D. Pa., motion to dismiss denied Feb 2025; direct-purchaser lenders). The senators' letter confirms price hikes and 'about half of states' but names no exclusive partners (ADP and Intuit not confirmed). Truv state contract not confirmed.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Consent-based competitors already hold state contracts (Washington, Missouri) at lower prices, states and integrators already orchestrate cheap sources first, and a router is a thin layer with a ceiling near $50M.

verdicts.title: Renewal Autopilot priced per auto-completed case

competitors_found.name: CMS vendor pledge group: Accenture, Acentra, Conduent, GDIT, Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Curam, Optum, RedMane
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pledged about $600M of free or discounted services to states for work requirements and redeterminations
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: Incumbent state eligibility-system and operations vendors

competitors_found.name: Maximus
competitors_found.what_they_do: Eligibility operations contractor; says growth in U.S. Services returns with Medicaid and SNAP requirements

competitors_found.name: Conduent work requirements suite
competitors_found.what_they_do: Determinations, reporting and compliance for community engagement

verdicts.substitutes: State staff; existing ex parte rules inside state eligibility systems; CMS free toolkit and Hub; Clarity Solutions-style mail-processing contracts.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: 55M renewals and recertifications at $12 per auto-completed case: $100M is 8.3M cases, which the idea itself puts at 30% of national volume at 50% auto-completion. No published per-renewal or outcome-based pricing or state RFP found. Savings logic ($55 per case) is plausible but the 2027 start is January 1 not July, and the vendor must integrate with systems owned by the incumbents.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: States sign outcome contracts against a measured baseline (no precedent found); incumbents allow third-party access to their eligibility systems (low); 10-15% national volume captured (heroic).
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Six-month renewals for expansion adults from 2027 confirmed (CMS guidance March 2026; two transition options). Staff-decides model is consistent with the rule. State procurement of outcome-priced operations is the untested premise.
verdicts.deciding_reason: Ten incumbents already pledged free or discounted help on the same systems the vendor needs access to; no outcome-pricing precedent; the idea's own $100M path needs heroic share.

competitors_found.name: Wipro MCAID360

verdicts.revenue_math_check: The idea's own total is $77-111M at near-total adoption of both halves. The code-set licence ($0.8-1.2M x 40 states) is undercut by a free equivalent. The clinician packet at $45 for 1.0-1.4M claimants is a thin-margin services network. Realistic median a handful of states.
